Considering fewer features at each split slightly lowers individual-tree accuracy but reduces correlation among trees; considering all features makes the method resemble ordinary bagged trees and lowers training time only marginally.

statements.text: The following claim is false: Lower individual-tree accuracy can be acceptable if the resulting diversity improves the aggregate.
statements.explanation: Ensemble quality depends on both member strength and error correlation.

statements.text: Considering all available features at every split removes the random-feature component of the forest.
statements.explanation: The method then relies on bootstrap variation but not feature subsampling at splits.

statements.text: The number of candidate features per split is a tradeoff between tree strength and diversity.
statements.explanation: Too many candidates can correlate trees; too few can weaken them excessively.

statements.text: Selecting fewer candidate features guarantees lower ensemble test error.
statements.explanation: The best setting depends on the data and must be validated.

statements.text: Inference cost and latency can increase as the number of trees grows.
statements.explanation: More trees generally require more split traversals and aggregation work at prediction time. G4: Diversity Among Learners

ML-D7G3Q3.subject: ML

ML-D7G4Q1.scenario: A model committee evaluates two ﬁve-model ensembles. Ensemble A contains ﬁve versions of the same tree that make almost identical mistakes; Ensemble B contains useful models whose errors occur on different observations. The committee chair asks which ensemble is more likely to beneﬁt from averaging.

statements.text: Ensemble B has more opportunity for errors to cancel.
statements.explanation: Different error patterns provide error-cancellation opportunities.

statements.text: Ensemble A effectively gains ﬁve independent sources of information merely because it contains ﬁve ﬁles.
statements.explanation: Duplicate or nearly identical models add little independent information.

statements.text: Diversity is useful only when the diverse learners retain some predictive skill.
statements.explanation: Diversity without useful signal can simply inject noise.

statements.text: Deliberately adding random but uninformative predictions must improve Ensemble B.
statements.explanation: Uninformative diversity can degrade the combined forecast.

statements.text: Comparing out-of-sample prediction or residual correlations can help distinguish the ensembles.
statements.explanation: Correlations reveal whether learners behave differently where it matters.

ML-D7G4Q1.subject: ML

ML-D7G4Q2.scenario: A global asset manager combines a linear model, KNN, and a decision tree to forecast returns. The CIO likes their architectural differences, but the validation report shows that all three make large errors on the same crisis dates because none was trained on comparable regimes. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Different algorithm names do not guarantee diverse prediction errors.
statements.explanation: Distinct methods may still learn similar signals or fail on the same cases.

statements.text: Shared blind spots can limit the ensemble’s protection during crisis periods.
statements.explanation: A common regime gap creates correlated errors.

statements.text: Averaging must eliminate an error that all three models make in the same direction.
statements.explanation: A shared directional error survives aggregation.

statements.text: Diversity should be assessed using model behavior, not architecture labels alone.
statements.explanation: Out-of-sample predictions and errors provide more relevant evidence of diversity.

statements.text: Adding a model that performs differently on crisis observations could improve ensemble robustness if it also generalizes.
statements.explanation: Complementary, validated behavior can address an existing common weakness.

ML-D7G4Q2.subject: ML

ML-D7G4Q3.scenario: A portfolio team wants to assign ensemble weights. One model has the best standalone Sharpe ratio but is highly correlated with two existing members; another has a lower standalone Sharpe ratio but makes useful forecasts on dates when the existing members fail. The portfolio manager must balance individual quality against complementarity.

statements.text: Standalone performance alone is insufficient to determine a model’s ensemble contribution.
statements.explanation: Marginal value depends on interaction with existing members as well as individual skill.

statements.text: The lower-Sharpe model could add more incremental value because of its complementary errors.
statements.explanation: A complementary model may improve the combined forecast despite weaker standalone results.

statements.text: Giving the highest-performing model all the weight always maximizes out-of-sample ensemble performance.
statements.explanation: Concentrating weight can discard diversiﬁcation and may overﬁt model selection.

statements.text: Ensemble weights should be chosen using only in-sample ﬁt because correlations are stable.
statements.explanation: In-sample relationships may be optimistic or unstable.

statements.text: Validation can compare whether weighting schemes improve the aggregate rather than merely its components.
statements.explanation: The ﬁnal combined model is the object that should be evaluated out of sample. G5: Boosting Intuition

ML-D7G4Q3.subject: ML

ML-D7G5Q1.scenario: A quant team builds a sequence of shallow regression trees to forecast returns. After the ﬁrst tree, the next tree is trained to address the remaining prediction errors, and the research lead explains that the ﬁnal forecast adds the trees’ contributions using a learning rate.

statements.text: Later trees are trained with information about errors left by earlier trees.
statements.explanation: Boosting focuses successive learners on what the current ensemble has not captured.

statements.text: This sequential dependence differs from standard bagging, where base learners can be trained independently.
statements.explanation: Bagged learners do not ordinarily depend on prior learners’ errors.

statements.text: The ﬁrst tree must perfectly ﬁt the targets before the second tree is useful.
statements.explanation: Remaining error is precisely what later learners are intended to reduce.

statements.text: A smaller learning rate can make each new tree’s correction more conservative.
statements.explanation: Shrinkage scales each added contribution.

statements.text: The ﬁnal boosted prediction necessarily equals an unweighted majority vote.
statements.explanation: Regression boosting commonly forms an additive, weighted prediction.

ML-D7G5Q1.subject: ML

ML-D7G5Q2.scenario: A fraud-detection desk uses a boosted classiﬁer. After an early model misses several rare manipulative orders, subsequent learners place greater emphasis on difficult or misclassiﬁed cases; the compliance director asks whether this means those cases are simply duplicated at prediction time. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Boosting can shift training attention toward examples the current ensemble handles poorly.
statements.explanation: Some boosting methods reweight hard cases, while others ﬁt residual-like errors.

statements.text: Emphasizing hard examples is a training mechanism, not a requirement to duplicate live observations at inference.
statements.explanation: Live predictions use the learned ensemble; the training emphasis need not alter incoming data.

statements.text: Later learners are designed to be exact independent copies of the ﬁrst learner.
statements.explanation: Later learners respond to the current ensemble’s weaknesses.

statements.text: A mislabeled training example may receive increasing attention and become harmful.
statements.explanation: Noise or bad labels can look persistently difficult and attract excessive focus.

statements.text: Boosting and bagging use the same sequential error-correction logic.
statements.explanation: Standard bagging trains learners independently on resampled data.

ML-D7G5Q2.subject: ML

ML-D7G5Q3.scenario: A portfolio manager compares a bagged-tree model and a boosted-tree model under a ﬁxed compute budget. The bagged trees train in parallel and mainly stabilize unstable estimates; the boosted trees train sequentially and progressively reﬁne the current prediction.

statements.text: Bagging is naturally easier to parallelize across base learners than sequential boosting.
statements.explanation: Bagged learners can be ﬁt separately, whereas each boosting stage depends on the current model.

statements.text: Boosting can reduce systematic error by building corrections to the current ensemble.
statements.explanation: Sequential corrections can ﬁt patterns a single weak learner misses.

statements.text: Bagging requires each new tree to ﬁt the residuals of all earlier trees.
statements.explanation: Residual-focused sequential ﬁtting characterizes boosting, not ordinary bagging.

statements.text: Boosting may use shallow trees as weak learners whose combined output is expressive.
statements.explanation: Many limited learners can form a strong nonlinear additive model.

statements.text: The two methods are guaranteed to produce identical forecasts if they use the same number of trees.
statements.explanation: Their sampling, ﬁtting, and aggregation procedures differ. G6: Bias vs. Variance in Ensembles

ML-D7G5Q3.subject: ML

ML-D7G6Q1.scenario: A research director repeatedly retrains a deep decision tree on slightly different samples and observes large changes in forecasts. A bagged ensemble of such trees produces much more consistent predictions, although both models retain a tendency to underestimate returns after major policy announcements. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: The single deep tree exhibits high variance across training samples.
statements.explanation: Large prediction changes from small sample changes indicate variance.

statements.text: Bagging can reduce the sample sensitivity of the aggregate.
statements.explanation: Averaging smooths learner-speciﬁc ﬂuctuations.

statements.text: The persistent underestimation suggests a bias that averaging similar trees may not remove.
statements.explanation: A common systematic error can remain after averaging.

statements.text: Reduced variance guarantees that the ensemble is unbiased.
statements.explanation: Variance and bias are distinct; improving one does not ensure the other is zero.

statements.text: Stability across retraining samples and accuracy relative to true targets describe different properties.
statements.explanation: A consistently wrong model can be stable, while an accurate-on-average model can be variable.

ML-D7G6Q1.subject: ML

ML-D7G6Q2.scenario: A desk averages 200 very shallow trees, each constrained so heavily that it predicts almost the same value for every market state. The head of research expects the large ensemble to recover the nonlinear structure that no member learned.

statements.text: Averaging can reduce variance but cannot create missing signal when all learners make nearly the same underﬁt prediction.
statements.explanation: Aggregation cannot recover structure absent from every prediction.

statements.text: Strongly underﬁt base learners can give the ensemble high bias.
statements.explanation: Excessive constraints can prevent the learners from capturing the relationship.

statements.text: Merely increasing the number of identical shallow trees must eliminate the bias.
statements.explanation: Repeating the same biased prediction preserves that bias.

statements.text: Boosting weak learners may reduce bias by adding sequential corrections, subject to tuning and data quality.
statements.explanation: Additive corrections can expand the model’s effective capacity.

statements.text: Out-of-sample evaluation is unnecessary once an ensemble contains 200 members.
statements.explanation: Ensemble size does not replace generalization testing.

ML-D7G6Q2.subject: ML

ML-D7G6Q3.scenario: A model-governance team compares three interventions: bagging unstable deep trees, boosting shallow trees that underﬁt, and averaging many copies of one deterministic linear model trained on identical data. The reviewer asks which changes address variance, which may address bias, and where beneﬁts are limited.

statements.text: Bagging the unstable trees is plausibly aimed at variance reduction.
statements.explanation: Resampling and aggregation can stabilize high-variance trees.

statements.text: Boosting shallow learners can reduce bias by building a more expressive combined model.
statements.explanation: Sequential additions can capture structure beyond one weak learner.

statements.text: Averaging identical predictions from the deterministic linear model changes the prediction.
statements.explanation: The average of identical values is that same value.

statements.text: If every ensemble member shares the same omitted-variable error, aggregation may leave it intact.
statements.explanation: Common systematic errors do not cancel.

statements.text: Bias and variance effects should be inferred solely from training error.
statements.explanation: Generalization behavior requires validation or other out-of-sample evidence. G7: Failure Modes of Ensembles

ML-D7G6Q3.subject: ML

ML-D7G7Q1.scenario: A hedge fund reports spectacular validation results from an ensemble that uses a “revised earnings” feature. An audit ﬁnds that the feature was populated with values released after each predicted trading date, and the CIO argues that averaging many models should protect the result from this problem.

statements.text: The ensemble’s reported performance may be driven by look-ahead leakage.
statements.explanation: Future-released values give the models information unavailable in real trading.

statements.text: Averaging many leaked models makes the information valid at the historical prediction time.
statements.explanation: Aggregation cannot repair invalid temporal availability.

statements.text: If all members exploit the leaked feature, their agreement can create false conﬁdence rather than independent conﬁrmation.
statements.explanation: Shared leakage produces correlated, systematically optimistic predictions.

statements.text: The feature should be reconstructed using only values available as of each prediction timestamp.
statements.explanation: Point-in-time data are necessary for a realistic evaluation.

statements.text: Strong ensemble performance eliminates the need to audit data provenance.
statements.explanation: Unexpectedly strong results make leakage review especially important.

ML-D7G7Q1.subject: ML

ML-D7G7Q2.scenario: A boosted trading model keeps adding trees until training error is almost zero. Validation performance peaks after 80 trees and then deteriorates, especially around noisy news events; the portfolio manager wants to deploy the 600-tree endpoint because it ﬁts history best. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: The divergence between falling training error and worsening validation performance is evidence of overﬁtting.
statements.explanation: The added ﬁt is not transferring to unseen data.

statements.text: Later boosting stages may focus excessively on noise or outliers.
statements.explanation: Persistently hard noisy cases can attract later corrections.

statements.text: Selecting the number of boosting stages using time-aware validation could improve generalization.
statements.explanation: Validation can identify a useful stopping region without relying on ﬁnal training ﬁt.

statements.text: Zero training error guarantees the smallest future trading loss.
statements.explanation: Perfect historical ﬁt can reﬂect memorization.

statements.text: Regularization choices such as learning rate, tree depth, or early stopping can affect the failure mode.
statements.explanation: These controls limit the size or aggressiveness of sequential corrections.

ML-D7G7Q2.subject: ML

ML-D7G7Q3.scenario: A risk ensemble contains 50 trees trained with nearly identical samples and the same dominant features. During a sudden liquidity regime change, all 50 underestimate transaction costs, while the risk officer had assumed the large model count guaranteed diversiﬁcation.

statements.text: The following claim is false: A large number of members does not guarantee meaningful model diversity.
statements.explanation: Effective diversity concerns behavior and errors, not just member count.

statements.text: Highly correlated errors can cause the full ensemble to fail together.
statements.explanation: Common errors survive aggregation.

statements.text: Averaging 50 underestimates must produce an unbiased cost estimate.
statements.explanation: An average of systematically low estimates can remain systematically low.

statements.text: Regime shift can expose a weakness shared by every learner because their training experience was similar.
statements.explanation: Shared data and features can lead to the same extrapolation failure.

statements.text: Stress testing by regime can reveal vulnerabilities that average validation metrics may hide.
statements.explanation: Segment-level evaluation can uncover concentrated failures in adverse conditions.

ML-D7G7Q3.subject: ML

ML-D8G1Q1.group_title: Role of Train, Validation, and Test Sets
ML-D8G1Q1.scenario: A research team divides ten years of market data into a training period, a validation period, and a ﬁnal test period. It ﬁts candidate models on the training period, uses the validation period to select hyperparameters, and plans to report performance from the test period.

statements.text: The training set is used to estimate model parameters from observed examples.
statements.explanation: Training data are used to ﬁt parameters or learned structure.

statements.text: The validation set can support model and hyperparameter selection without directly ﬁtting the ﬁnal test observations.
statements.explanation: Validation data provide feedback for choices made before the ﬁnal test.

statements.text: The team should repeatedly inspect test results while revising features because the test data are not part of training.
statements.explanation: Repeatedly adapting to test results turns the test set into part of the development process.

statements.text: The test set is most informative as a ﬁnal evaluation when earlier decisions have not been adapted to its results.
statements.explanation: An untouched test set better represents a ﬁnal out-of-sample check.

statements.text: Having a validation set guarantees that the selected model will perform equally well in all future markets.
statements.explanation: Market shifts and sampling uncertainty prevent such a guarantee.

ML-D8G1Q1.subject: ML

ML-D8G1Q2.group_title: Role of Train, Validation, and Test Sets
ML-D8G1Q2.scenario: A student trains ﬁve decision-tree variants, chooses the depth with the lowest validation error, retrains that chosen conﬁguration on the combined training and validation periods, and then evaluates it once on a later test period.

statements.text: Using validation performance to choose tree depth is an appropriate role for the validation set.
statements.explanation: Hyperparameter selection is a standard use of validation data.

statements.text: Retraining the chosen conﬁguration on training plus validation data can be reasonable if the test set remains untouched.
statements.explanation: After selection, more pre-test data may be used to ﬁt the ﬁnal model.

statements.text: The test score should be used to choose a different depth whenever it is disappointing.
statements.explanation: Changing depth in response to test performance contaminates the ﬁnal evaluation.

statements.text: A later test period can better respect temporal order than a random mixture of earlier and later observations.
statements.explanation: Evaluating on a later period avoids training on observations from the test period’s future.

statements.text: Model selection on validation data means the validation score is completely free of selection optimism.
statements.explanation: Trying many alternatives can produce an optimistically low validation error.

ML-D8G1Q2.subject: ML

ML-D8G1Q3.group_title: Role of Train, Validation, and Test Sets
ML-D8G1Q3.scenario: A small trading project has only three years of observations. To preserve data, the analyst skips validation, selects features and model settings by repeatedly checking the test score, and then presents the best observed test result as an unbiased estimate of future performance. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Repeated test-set feedback can inﬂuence the analyst’s choices even if the test rows are never passed to the model’s ﬁt method.
statements.explanation: Human decisions based on test feedback create indirect adaptation to the test set.

statements.text: The reported best test result may be optimistic because the analyst selected it after many attempts.
statements.explanation: Selecting the best of repeated trials exploits chance variation in that particular set.

statements.text: A separate validation procedure could reduce the amount of model-selection pressure placed on the ﬁnal test set.
statements.explanation: Validation data can guide development while reserving the test set for ﬁnal evaluation.

statements.text: A small dataset makes test-set reuse harmless because fewer observations are available.
statements.explanation: Scarce data do not eliminate contamination and may make estimates even less stable.

statements.text: The labels of the test observations must be available to calculate prediction error, but they need not be used to ﬁt or tune the model.
statements.explanation: Test labels are needed for scoring but should remain outside ﬁtting and tuning. G2: Error Metrics – MAE, MSE, RMSE

ML-D8G1Q3.subject: ML

ML-D8G2Q1.scenario: A client reviewing your model asks why RMSE is used instead of MAE. The risk team is concerned about large prediction errors during volatile periods.

statements.text: MSE penalizes large errors more than MAE.
statements.explanation: The squared term ampliﬁes large errors.

statements.text: RMSE is less sensitive to outliers than MAE.
statements.explanation: RMSE is more sensitive to large errors and outliers.

statements.text: MAE treats all errors equally.
statements.explanation: MAE applies a linear penalty to absolute error magnitude.

statements.text: RMSE has the same units as the target variable.
statements.explanation: Taking the square root restores the target variable’s units.

statements.text: RMSE highlights large errors more than MAE.
statements.explanation: Squaring before averaging places greater emphasis on large deviations.

ML-D8G2Q1.subject: ML

ML-D8G2Q2.scenario: Two return-forecasting models are evaluated on the same days. Most errors are small, but Model A makes one exceptionally large error during a market shock. The team compares MAE, MSE, and RMSE. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: The exceptionally large error will generally have more inﬂuence on MSE than on MAE.
statements.explanation: Quadratic loss gives disproportionate weight to a very large miss.

statements.text: RMSE and MAE can rank the two models differently because they weight error magnitudes differently.
statements.explanation: A model with typical small errors but one large miss may look better under MAE and worse under RMSE.

statements.text: Squaring errors in MSE prevents positive and negative errors from canceling.
statements.explanation: Squared errors are nonnegative regardless of error direction.

statements.text: RMSE must always be numerically smaller than MAE on the same predictions.
statements.explanation: RMSE is generally at least as large as MAE for the same set of errors.

statements.text: Removing the shock day solely because it hurts Model A would change the evaluation question and could bias the comparison.
statements.explanation: Selective removal based on one model’s performance compromises a fair assessment.

ML-D8G2Q2.subject: ML

ML-D8G2Q3.scenario: A model predicts daily dollar proﬁt for a strategy. Its MAE is $400, its MSE is 490,000 dollars squared, and its RMSE is $700. A manager wants to interpret these values and decide which loss function reﬂects operational concerns.

statements.text: The MAE indicates an average absolute prediction error of $400.
statements.explanation: MAE averages the absolute dollar errors.

statements.text: The MSE is expressed in dollars, just like the target.
statements.explanation: MSE has squared units, here dollars squared.

statements.text: The RMSE is expressed in dollars and is therefore easier to compare directly with the target scale than MSE.
statements.explanation: RMSE returns the error measure to the original target units.

statements.text: The fact that RMSE exceeds MAE is consistent with variation in the sizes of the errors.
statements.explanation: Larger dispersion in absolute errors tends to widen the gap between RMSE and MAE.

statements.text: Choosing MAE rather than RMSE is purely mathematical and need not reﬂect how costly large misses are.
statements.explanation: Metric choice should reﬂect whether error costs grow linearly or place extra weight on large misses. G3: Baselines and Benchmarking

ML-D8G2Q3.subject: ML

ML-D8G3Q1.scenario: A regression model predicts next-day returns with an RMSE of 0.012. The team celebrates the low number, but it has not compared the model with a predictor that always outputs the training-set mean return.

statements.text: The RMSE value alone does not show whether the model improves on a simple baseline.
statements.explanation: The magnitude needs context from the target scale and a relevant comparator.

statements.text: A mean-prediction baseline provides a reference for judging whether the model captures useful predictive structure under squared-error evaluation.
statements.explanation: Predicting the training mean is a simple benchmark for squared-error regression.

statements.text: If the model’s test RMSE is worse than the baseline’s on the same observations, the model has not added value according to that metric.
statements.explanation: Higher RMSE indicates worse performance under that evaluation criterion.

statements.text: A baseline must use a more complex algorithm than the candidate model to be informative.
statements.explanation: Baselines are often deliberately simple.

statements.text: The baseline’s mean should be calculated using the test targets before predictions are made.
statements.explanation: Using test targets to construct predictions leaks information from the evaluation set.

ML-D8G3Q1.subject: ML

ML-D8G3Q2.scenario: A classiﬁer predicts whether tomorrow’s market return will be positive. Because 60% of test days are positive, an always- up rule achieves 60% accuracy, while the new model achieves 58%.

statements.text: The always-up rule is a relevant naive accuracy baseline for this imbalanced outcome.
statements.explanation: Always predicting the majority class establishes a simple reference accuracy.

statements.text: The model’s 58% accuracy beats the always-up baseline because it uses features.
statements.explanation: Fifty-eight percent is below the baseline’s 60% on this metric.

statements.text: Comparing against the baseline reveals information that the model’s accuracy alone does not.
statements.explanation: The comparison shows that apparent predictive accuracy may not exceed a trivial rule.

statements.text: The model might still be useful under a different objective, but that claim would require an appropriate metric and evidence.
statements.explanation: For example, asymmetric payoffs could matter, but they must be evaluated rather than assumed.

statements.text: A sophisticated model is automatically preferable to a naive rule even when it performs worse on the stated objective.
statements.explanation: Complexity alone does not establish value.

ML-D8G3Q2.subject: ML

ML-D8G3Q3.scenario: A trading team compares a learned strategy with buy-and-hold. The learned strategy has a higher cumulative return in the test period but also takes substantially more risk and incurs frequent transaction costs that were omitted from the simulation. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Buy-and-hold can serve as one useful benchmark for a trading strategy.
statements.explanation: It represents a simple investable alternative for comparison.

statements.text: Higher raw return alone proves the learned strategy is superior under every reasonable objective.
statements.explanation: Risk, costs, drawdowns, and the investor’s objective can change the conclusion.

statements.text: A cash or no-trade benchmark may provide additional context beyond buy-and-hold.
statements.explanation: Multiple simple alternatives can reveal what kind of value the strategy adds.

statements.text: Omitting transaction costs can overstate the apparent value added by a high-turnover strategy.
statements.explanation: Frequent trading magniﬁes the effect of unmodeled costs.

statements.text: Benchmarks should be evaluated over the same market period as the learned strategy when making a direct comparison.
statements.explanation: A common period controls for differences in market conditions. G4: Fair Model Comparison

ML-D8G3Q3.subject: ML

ML-D8G4Q1.scenario: Two analysts compare a linear model and a decision tree. The linear model is tested on a calm recent year, while the tree is tested on an earlier crisis year. Both report RMSE, and the team declares the model with the lower value the winner.

statements.text: Using different test periods confounds model quality with differences in market conditions.
statements.explanation: One period may be intrinsically harder to predict than the other.

statements.text: The models should generally be scored on the same held-out observations for a direct comparison.
statements.explanation: Common observations provide a consistent evaluation challenge.

statements.text: Using RMSE for both models is sufficient to make the comparison fair despite different test data.
statements.explanation: A common metric does not correct for unequal test conditions.

statements.text: A paired comparison on the same observations can reveal which model errs on particular cases.
statements.explanation: Matching observations supports case-by-case analysis of error differences.

statements.text: The crisis-period model must be better if it was trained with more rows.
statements.explanation: Training-set size alone does not establish test performance.

ML-D8G4Q1.subject: ML

ML-D8G4Q2.scenario: A team compares KNN with a regression tree. It standardizes all features using means and standard deviations computed from the full dataset before splitting, then trains both models and reports test error. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Computing scaling statistics from the full dataset exposes the comparison to information from the test set.
statements.explanation: The preprocessing step uses the distribution of held-out observations.

statements.text: Scaling parameters should be estimated from the training data and then applied unchanged to validation and test data.
statements.explanation: This keeps test information out of the ﬁtted transformation.

statements.text: Because trees are usually insensitive to monotonic feature scaling, leakage in the shared preprocessing is acceptable.
statements.explanation: Test leakage remains a methodological ﬂaw even if one learner is less sensitive to scaling.

statements.text: Applying a consistent, leakage-free preprocessing protocol supports a fairer comparison.
statements.explanation: Models should be compared under a valid protocol appropriate to each learner.

statements.text: KNN may be affected more directly by feature scaling than a decision tree because KNN relies on distances.
statements.explanation: Scale affects the relative contribution of features to KNN distance.

ML-D8G4Q2.subject: ML

ML-D8G4Q3.scenario: A researcher reports MAE for Model A and RMSE for Model B, then selects whichever displayed number is smaller. Model A predicts in percentage points, while Model B’s output was converted to decimal returns.

statements.text: Comparing the displayed MAE and RMSE values directly mixes different loss deﬁnitions.
statements.explanation: MAE and RMSE weight the error distribution differently.

statements.text: Different output units make the raw numerical values incomparable without conversion.
statements.explanation: One percentage point equals 0.01 in decimal-return units.

statements.text: Both models should be evaluated with the same chosen metric and units on the same observations for a direct ranking.
statements.explanation: Consistency isolates model performance from evaluation choices.

statements.text: A smaller displayed number always means better predictions regardless of metric and scale.
statements.explanation: Metric deﬁnition and units determine what a number means.

statements.text: It can be reasonable to report multiple metrics, provided each metric is calculated consistently for both models and interpreted separately.
statements.explanation: Multiple consistently calculated measures can illuminate different tradeoffs. G5: Metric Selection and Business Alignment

ML-D8G4Q3.subject: ML

ML-D8G5Q1.scenario: A model has excellent next-day price RMSE, but a strategy that trades on its forecasts loses money after bid-ask spreads, commissions, and market impact. The research lead argues that prediction accuracy is all that matters. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Low prediction RMSE does not guarantee proﬁtable trading after costs.
statements.explanation: Execution costs and decision rules intervene between predictions and proﬁt.

statements.text: A trading-oriented evaluation may need to include returns, risk, turnover, and transaction costs.
statements.explanation: These measures connect evaluation to the deployed objective and constraints.

statements.text: Improving RMSE by correcting small forecasts that never change a trade can have little effect on strategy performance.
statements.explanation: A statistical improvement need not alter any economically relevant decision.

statements.text: Statistical prediction metrics should be discarded entirely whenever the ﬁnal application is trading.
statements.explanation: Prediction metrics remain diagnostically useful even when they are not sufficient.

statements.text: The evaluation criterion should reﬂect how model outputs are converted into positions and outcomes.
statements.explanation: Business value depends on the full decision pipeline.

ML-D8G5Q1.subject: ML

ML-D8G5Q2.scenario: A risk system predicts daily portfolio losses. The ﬁrm considers a $100 error on an ordinary day manageable but views a $10,000 underestimate during a stressed day as especially dangerous.

statements.text: An error measure that places extra weight on large misses may better reﬂect the stated concern than MAE alone.
statements.explanation: The ﬁrm assigns disproportionate importance to severe misses.

statements.text: MSE or RMSE can emphasize large absolute errors through squaring.
statements.explanation: Squaring magniﬁes the contribution of large errors.

statements.text: A symmetric metric treats overestimates and underestimates of equal magnitude the same, even if the ﬁrm considers underestimation more harmful.
statements.explanation: MAE, MSE, and RMSE do not distinguish error direction by themselves.

statements.text: The lowest average error automatically identiﬁes the safest model under all tail-risk objectives.
statements.explanation: Average performance can conceal dangerous behavior in critical cases.

statements.text: The team may need an asymmetric or tail-focused evaluation in addition to standard aggregate error metrics.
statements.explanation: Additional measures can capture the ﬁrm’s unequal and tail-speciﬁc costs.

ML-D8G5Q2.subject: ML

ML-D8G5Q3.scenario: A model predicts the correct direction of tomorrow’s return on 55% of days. Most correct calls occur on tiny moves, while it is often wrong on large moves. Another model has 52% directional accuracy but captures several large proﬁtable moves. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Directional accuracy weights each day equally regardless of the size of the market move.
statements.explanation: A correct tiny move and a correct large move each count as one correct classiﬁcation.

statements.text: The 55% model must produce the greater trading proﬁt because it is correct more often.
statements.explanation: Frequency of correct direction does not determine the payoff magnitude.

statements.text: Return magnitude, position sizing, and trading costs can make the 52% model more economically valuable.
statements.explanation: Trading outcomes depend on more than the percentage of correct signs.

statements.text: Evaluating only directional accuracy may be misaligned with a proﬁt-oriented objective.
statements.explanation: The metric may ignore the consequences of being right or wrong.

statements.text: Choosing an economically aligned metric removes the need to evaluate the strategy out of sample.
statements.explanation: Any chosen metric still requires disciplined out-of-sample evaluation. G6: Variability and Stability of Results

ML-D8G5Q3.subject: ML

ML-D8G6Q1.scenario: A decision tree achieves test RMSE values of 0.010, 0.011, 0.029, 0.013, and 0.026 across ﬁve reasonable time-based splits. The analyst wants to report only the lowest value because it demonstrates the model’s potential. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: The range of results suggests that performance is sensitive to the evaluation period.
statements.explanation: The errors vary substantially across plausible evaluation windows.

statements.text: Reporting only 0.010 would conceal important information about variability.
statements.explanation: The selected result is not representative of all reported trials.

statements.text: Summarizing both central performance and dispersion across splits gives a fuller picture than reporting the best run alone.
statements.explanation: Typical performance and uncertainty are both relevant to reliability.

statements.text: Variation across splits proves that every implementation of the model is incorrect.
statements.explanation: Variation can arise from sampling and regime differences without an implementation defect.

statements.text: Differences in market regimes could contribute to the observed instability.
statements.explanation: Market relationships and volatility can change over time.

ML-D8G6Q1.subject: ML

ML-D8G6Q2.scenario: A bagged learner is retrained ten times using different random seeds. Its validation scores are nearly identical, while a single deep tree’s scores vary widely. Their average validation errors are similar.

statements.text: The bagged learner appears more stable with respect to the tested source of randomness.
statements.explanation: Its scores change little when the seed changes.

statements.text: Similar average error means the two models have identical reliability.
statements.explanation: Models with the same mean can have very different dispersion.

statements.text: Random seeds should be recorded when they affect resampling or model construction.
statements.explanation: Recording seeds improves reproducibility and clariﬁes experimental conditions.

statements.text: Repeated runs can help distinguish a typical result from a lucky initialization or sample.
statements.explanation: Multiple runs reveal sensitivity that a single outcome cannot.

statements.text: Low variation across seeds guarantees stability under future changes in market regime.
statements.explanation: Seed stability does not test robustness to distributional change.

ML-D8G6Q2.subject: ML

ML-D8G6Q3.scenario: Two models have the same mean out-of-sample MAE across six sequential test windows. Model A’s MAE is similar in every window, while Model B is excellent in four windows and very poor in two volatile windows. The system will be used where large performance swings are costly.

statements.text: Equal mean MAE does not imply equal stability across windows.
statements.explanation: The same average can arise from different distributions of performance.

statements.text: Model A may be preferable if consistency is an important operational objective.
statements.explanation: Lower variability aligns with the stated cost of large swings.

statements.text: Examining window-level results can reveal failure patterns hidden by the overall average.
statements.explanation: Aggregation can conceal regime-speciﬁc weakness.

statements.text: Model B’s strong performance in four windows guarantees that its two poor windows are irrelevant.
statements.explanation: Poor performance during volatile periods may be operationally important.

statements.text: The choice between the models may reasonably depend on both average error and variability.
statements.explanation: Evaluation should reﬂect typical accuracy and stability requirements.

ML-D8G6Q3.subject: ML

ML-D9G1Q1.scenario: Your team presents a model with near-zero training error but much worse performance on new data. The PM asks whether this is acceptable.

statements.text: This indicates overﬁtting.
statements.explanation: Near-zero training error combined with poor performance on new data is the classic overﬁtting pattern.

statements.text: The model likely has high variance.
statements.explanation: Strong sensitivity to the particular training sample is characteristic of high variance.

statements.text: Increasing training data may help.
statements.explanation: More representative training data can make it harder for the model to ﬁt sample-speciﬁc noise.

statements.text: Reducing model complexity may help.
statements.explanation: Reducing capacity can limit the model’s ability to ﬁt noise.

statements.text: This indicates underﬁtting.
statements.explanation: Underﬁtting normally produces poor performance even on the training data.

ML-D9G1Q1.subject: ML

ML-D9G1Q2.scenario: A student ﬁts a shallow decision tree to a nonlinear relationship between market indicators and next-day returns. Both training and test errors are high and similar, and increasing the training sample without changing the tree produces little improvement.

statements.text: The similar, high training and test errors are consistent with underﬁtting.
statements.explanation: Underﬁt models often perform poorly on both seen and unseen observations.

statements.text: The tree may have insufficient capacity to represent the relevant relationship.
statements.explanation: A tree that is too shallow may be unable to express an important nonlinear pattern.

statements.text: Making the tree shallower would necessarily correct the problem.
statements.explanation: Further reducing capacity would generally worsen an underﬁtting problem.

statements.text: A modest increase in model complexity could reduce bias.
statements.explanation: Additional capacity may capture structure that the current model misses.

statements.text: A small train–test gap by itself proves that the model generalizes well.
statements.explanation: Two similarly poor scores indicate consistency, not useful predictive performance.

ML-D9G1Q2.subject: ML

ML-D9G1Q3.scenario: Three models are evaluated on the same return-prediction task. Model A has high training and high validation error. Model B has very low training error but high validation error. Model C has moderate, similar training and validation error and outperforms both on validation data.

statements.text: Model A shows a pattern consistent with underﬁtting.
statements.explanation: High error even on training data suggests that Model A is not capturing enough structure.

statements.text: Model B shows a pattern consistent with overﬁtting.
statements.explanation: Excellent training ﬁt with poor validation performance is a standard overﬁtting symptom.

statements.text: Model C currently provides the strongest evidence of generalization among the three.
statements.explanation: Model C has the best validation performance without a large gap from training performance.

statements.text: Model B should be preferred because the lowest training error always identiﬁes the best model.
statements.explanation: Training error alone rewards memorization and does not establish performance on new data.

statements.text: The train–validation gap is useful only for classiﬁcation models, not regression models.
statements.explanation: Training and validation behavior is informative for both regression and classiﬁcation. G2: Bias–Variance Tradeoff

ML-D9G1Q3.subject: ML

ML-D9G2Q1.scenario: An analyst gradually increases the maximum depth of a decision tree. Training error falls at every step, while validation error ﬁrst falls and then rises after the tree becomes deep. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: The shallowest trees may have relatively high bias.
statements.explanation: Very limited trees may systematically miss useful structure.

statements.text: Very deep trees may have relatively high variance.
statements.explanation: Deep trees can become sensitive to noise and small changes in the training set.

statements.text: The depth with the lowest validation error may be a better choice than the depth with the lowest training error.
statements.explanation: Validation performance better reﬂects the goal of performing well on unseen data.

statements.text: Increasing depth must reduce both bias and variance simultaneously.
statements.explanation: Greater capacity often reduces bias while increasing variance.

statements.text: The rise in validation error suggests that additional capacity has begun to harm generalization.
statements.explanation: Worsening validation performance despite improving training ﬁt is evidence of overﬁtting.

ML-D9G2Q1.subject: ML

ML-D9G2Q2.scenario: A team compares a straight-line model with a ﬂexible nonlinear learner across many independently sampled training sets. The linear model makes similar predictions each time but repeatedly misses a curved relationship. The nonlinear learner ﬁts the curve on average but changes substantially across samples. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: The linear model’s systematic miss is evidence of relatively high bias.
statements.explanation: Repeatedly missing the same structural pattern indicates systematic error.

statements.text: The nonlinear learner’s sensitivity across samples is evidence of relatively high variance.
statements.explanation: Large prediction changes across plausible training samples indicate variance.

statements.text: A model can have low variance yet still make consistently inaccurate predictions.
statements.explanation: Stable predictions can be consistently wrong when the model is too restrictive.

statements.text: High variance means that a model must have high training error on every sample.
statements.explanation: A high-variance model can ﬁt each training set extremely well while generalizing poorly.

statements.text: Model selection should consider expected out-of-sample error rather than minimizing either bias or variance in isolation.
statements.explanation: Useful selection balances sources of error according to performance on new observations.

ML-D9G2Q2.subject: ML

ML-D9G2Q3.scenario: A KNN regressor is tested with several values of k. With k = 1, predictions follow individual training observations closely. With a very large k, predictions are nearly constant across the feature space.

statements.text: The k = 1 model will generally have lower training error than the very-large-k model.
statements.explanation: A point can be its own nearest neighbor, producing extremely close training ﬁts.

statements.text: Increasing k usually smooths the prediction function.
statements.explanation: Each prediction averages over a broader neighborhood as k grows.

statements.text: A very large k can increase bias by averaging away local structure.
statements.explanation: Excessive smoothing may miss real local relationships.

statements.text: A very small k can increase variance by making predictions sensitive to individual observations.
statements.explanation: Predictions based on very few neighbors can change sharply with the sample.

statements.text: Increasing k always increases model capacity.
statements.explanation: Larger k generally reduces the effective ﬂexibility or capacity of KNN. G3: Model Capacity vs. Data Size

ML-D9G2Q3.subject: ML

ML-D9G3Q1.scenario: A deep decision tree overﬁts a training set containing only 300 trading days. The team can collect several years of comparable observations from the same data-generating process.

statements.text: Additional representative data may reduce the tree’s tendency to ﬁt peculiarities of the original small sample.
statements.explanation: A larger representative sample can reduce sensitivity to accidental patterns in a small dataset.

statements.text: More observations can make estimates of recurring patterns more reliable.
statements.explanation: Repeated evidence helps distinguish persistent structure from noise.

statements.text: Adding duplicated copies of the same 300 rows provides the same beneﬁt as collecting genuinely new observations.
statements.explanation: Duplicates add no independent information about the underlying relationship.

statements.text: More data guarantees that an arbitrarily complex model cannot overﬁt.
statements.explanation: Excessive capacity, noise, leakage, or poor sampling can still produce overﬁtting.

statements.text: The usefulness of additional data depends partly on whether it represents the deployment setting.
statements.explanation: Large but unrepresentative datasets may not improve performance where the model is used.

ML-D9G3Q1.subject: ML

ML-D9G3Q2.scenario: A linear model underﬁts a strongly curved relationship. The analyst adds one million more observations from the same relationship but retains exactly the same linear feature representation and model form. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: More data alone may not remove error caused by an inability to represent the curve.
statements.explanation: Additional examples do not change the functions the model class can express.

statements.text: The model’s limitation is primarily one of capacity rather than sample size.
statements.explanation: The speciﬁed linear form cannot capture the relevant curvature.

statements.text: A richer feature representation or a more expressive model may be needed.
statements.explanation: Greater representational capacity may reduce this systematic error.

statements.text: With enough data, every model class can represent every possible target function.
statements.explanation: Data quantity does not eliminate restrictions imposed by the hypothesis class.

statements.text: The larger sample can still improve the precision with which the best linear approximation is estimated.
statements.explanation: More data can estimate the model’s parameters more reliably even if approximation bias remains.

ML-D9G3Q2.subject: ML

ML-D9G3Q3.scenario: Two teams train the same ﬂexible learner. Team A uses 500 clean, relevant observations. Team B uses 50,000 observations, but most come from an old market regime with different relationships from the intended deployment period.

statements.text: Team B’s larger row count does not automatically make its model more generalizable to the new regime.
statements.explanation: Quantity cannot fully compensate for observations drawn from the wrong distribution.

statements.text: Relevant sampling can matter as much as raw dataset size.
statements.explanation: The training examples should reﬂect the relationships the model will encounter.

statements.text: Historical regime mismatch can create poor deployment performance even when training error is low.
statements.explanation: A model may learn old-regime patterns that no longer apply.

statements.text: Team A must outperform Team B because smaller datasets always contain less bias.
statements.explanation: Neither sample size alone nor a general rule guarantees Team A’s superiority.

statements.text: Evaluating both models on representative out-of-sample data would help assess which dataset supports the intended use.
statements.explanation: A representative evaluation provides evidence about performance under the target conditions. G4: Cross-Validation and Generalization Estimation

ML-D9G3Q3.subject: ML

ML-D9G4Q1.scenario: A researcher performs ﬁve-fold cross-validation on a dataset. In each round, the model is trained on four folds and evaluated on the remaining fold, with each fold serving as the evaluation fold once.

statements.text: Each observation is used for evaluation in one of the ﬁve rounds.
statements.explanation: Every fold takes one turn as the held-out evaluation subset.

statements.text: Each ﬁtted model is trained on all ﬁve folds, including its evaluation fold.
statements.explanation: The evaluation fold is excluded from training in that round.

statements.text: Averaging the fold scores can provide a less split-speciﬁc estimate than relying on one arbitrary holdout.
statements.explanation: Multiple partitions reveal how performance changes with the split.

statements.text: Cross-validation produces ﬁve evaluations of one unchanged ﬁtted model.
statements.explanation: A separate model is ﬁtted for each training-fold combination.

statements.text: Model preprocessing that learns from data should be ﬁtted within each training portion rather than once on the full dataset.
statements.explanation: Fitting preprocessing globally can leak information from evaluation folds into training.

ML-D9G4Q1.subject: ML

ML-D9G4Q2.scenario: A student uses cross-validation to select tree depth from 20 alternatives. The student reports the best mean cross- validation score as the ﬁnal, unbiased estimate of performance and does not retain a separate test set. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Cross-validation can support the selection of tree depth.
statements.explanation: Comparing validation performance across depths is a valid use of cross-validation.

statements.text: Choosing the best of many alternatives can make the selected cross-validation score optimistic.
statements.explanation: Selection can exploit chance advantages in the folds used for tuning.

statements.text: A separate untouched test set can provide a stronger ﬁnal check after model selection.
statements.explanation: An untouched test set avoids reusing the same evidence for selection and ﬁnal assessment.

statements.text: Cross-validation guarantees that the selected depth will generalize equally well to all future periods.
statements.explanation: Sampling uncertainty and market change prevent such a guarantee.

statements.text: The folds should be constructed in a way that respects the structure of the data and prediction task.
statements.explanation: Time order or other dependencies may make ordinary random folds inappropriate.

ML-D9G4Q2.subject: ML

ML-D9G4Q3.scenario: A forecasting team randomly assigns daily observations from ten years of market data to cross-validation folds. As a result, models are sometimes trained on later dates and evaluated on earlier dates, even though deployment will predict the future from the past.

statements.text: Random folds can create an evaluation that does not match the temporal direction of deployment.
statements.explanation: The random split can allow future information to inﬂuence models evaluated on the past.

statements.text: Time-aware folds that train on earlier observations and validate on later observations may be more appropriate.
statements.explanation: Forward or rolling splits better mirror forecasting use.

statements.text: Using future observations for training can produce misleading estimates when relationships change over time.
statements.explanation: Regime changes can make access to later patterns an unrealistic advantage.

statements.text: Cross-validation is invalid for every time-series problem.
statements.explanation: Cross-validation can be adapted to preserve time order.

statements.text: More folds automatically correct any violation of temporal order.
statements.explanation: Increasing the fold count does not repair an inappropriate splitting design. G5: Detecting Overﬁtting in Practice

ML-D9G4Q3.subject: ML

ML-D9G5Q1.scenario: A model reports 99.9% directional accuracy on unseen market data, far above every prior experiment. The analyst discovers that features were normalized using statistics calculated from the full dataset and that one feature was constructed using the next day’s closing price. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: The extraordinary result should prompt checks for leakage and evaluation errors.
statements.explanation: Results that are implausibly strong warrant careful examination of data and procedure.

statements.text: Using the next day’s closing price to predict next-day direction gives the model information unavailable at decision time.
statements.explanation: The feature directly incorporates future information about the target period.

statements.text: Full-dataset normalization can contaminate the evaluation because test-period information inﬂuences preprocessing.
statements.explanation: Even unsupervised preprocessing should be learned without access to held-out observations.

statements.text: A very high score proves the model has discovered a durable market inefficiency.
statements.explanation: Leakage provides a more immediate explanation and the result requires validation.

statements.text: Rebuilding the pipeline using only information available at each training and prediction point is necessary for a credible assessment.
statements.explanation: The experiment must reproduce the information boundaries of actual use.

ML-D9G5Q1.subject: ML

ML-D9G5Q2.scenario: A single decision tree is retrained on ﬁve slightly different samples. Its training error remains near zero, but its chosen splits and out-of-sample returns change dramatically from run to run.

statements.text: The changing structure and performance are signs of model instability.
statements.explanation: Small data changes are producing large changes in the learned model and its results.

statements.text: Near-zero training error rules out overﬁtting.
statements.explanation: Extremely low training error can accompany severe overﬁtting.

statements.text: Sensitivity to small sample changes is consistent with high variance.
statements.explanation: Sample sensitivity is a deﬁning symptom of variance.

statements.text: Examining results across repeated samples reveals information that one run would hide.
statements.explanation: Repeated trials expose the range and reliability of performance.

statements.text: The most proﬁtable run should be reported alone because it shows the model’s true expected performance.
statements.explanation: Selecting the best run conceals variability and creates an optimistic impression.

ML-D9G5Q2.subject: ML

ML-D9G5Q3.scenario: An analyst tries 500 combinations of indicators, lookback periods, and model settings on one validation period. One combination earns an exceptional Sharpe ratio, but its training score is ordinary and its performance collapses on a later test period.

statements.text: Trying many alternatives increases the chance of ﬁnding a conﬁguration that beneﬁts from random validation noise.
statements.explanation: A broad search can identify a chance winner even when no durable advantage exists.

statements.text: The later test failure is consistent with selection overﬁtting.
statements.explanation: The selected conﬁguration may have adapted to peculiarities of the validation period.

statements.text: The best validation result among 500 trials is necessarily an unbiased estimate of future performance.
statements.explanation: Choosing the maximum observed score introduces selection optimism.

statements.text: Recording the full search process and evaluating the selected model on untouched data would improve the credibility of the conclusion.
statements.explanation: Transparency and fresh evaluation data help distinguish stable performance from data mining.

statements.text: An ordinary training score guarantees that the validation success was genuine.
statements.explanation: Training behavior does not validate an exceptional result found through repeated search. G6: Controlling Model Complexity

ML-D9G5Q3.subject: ML

ML-D9G6Q1.scenario: A deep decision tree ﬁts nearly every ﬂuctuation in the training data but performs poorly on validation data. The team considers reducing maximum depth and increasing the minimum number of observations required in each leaf. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Reducing maximum depth limits the number of successive splits the tree can make.
statements.explanation: A shallower tree has fewer levels available to partition the data.

statements.text: Increasing the minimum leaf size can prevent the tree from creating leaves for very small groups of observations.
statements.explanation: Larger leaves discourage highly speciﬁc partitions.

statements.text: Both changes can reduce the tree’s effective complexity.
statements.explanation: Each constraint limits the tree’s ability to ﬁt ﬁne-grained sample variation.

statements.text: These changes are guaranteed to improve test performance for every dataset.
statements.explanation: Excessive restriction can cause underﬁtting, and results depend on the data.

statements.text: Complexity controls should be selected using appropriate validation evidence rather than test-set feedback.
statements.explanation: The ﬁnal test set should remain independent of hyperparameter selection.

ML-D9G6Q1.subject: ML

ML-D9G6Q2.scenario: A team uses regularized linear regression with a penalty on large coefficient values. It gradually increases the penalty strength while monitoring training and validation error.

statements.text: The penalty discourages the model from relying on extremely large coefficients.
statements.explanation: Large coefficient magnitudes make the optimization objective more costly.

statements.text: Stronger regularization typically increases the freedom of the model to ﬁt the training data.
statements.explanation: A stronger penalty constrains the ﬁtted solution rather than increasing its freedom.

statements.text: Moderate regularization may improve generalization when the unregularized model has high variance.
statements.explanation: Accepting some additional bias can reduce variance and improve performance on new data.

statements.text: Excessively strong regularization can create underﬁtting.
statements.explanation: An overly restrictive penalty can suppress useful relationships.

statements.text: Regularization eliminates the need for validation because any positive penalty prevents overﬁtting.
statements.explanation: The appropriate penalty is data dependent and still requires disciplined selection and evaluation.

ML-D9G6Q2.subject: ML

ML-D9G6Q3.scenario: During iterative training, a learner’s training error keeps decreasing. Validation error decreases through iteration 40, then rises steadily while training continues to improve. The team considers early stopping.

statements.text: The divergence after iteration 40 suggests that later training is ﬁtting details that do not generalize.
statements.explanation: Continued training helps the training set while harming validation performance.

statements.text: Stopping near the best validation iteration can act as a form of complexity control.
statements.explanation: Limiting the number of iterations restricts how fully the learner adapts to the training sample.

statements.text: Selecting the stopping point by repeatedly examining the ﬁnal test set is appropriate.
statements.explanation: A validation set, not the ﬁnal test set, should guide the stopping decision.

statements.text: Training until training error is minimized must produce the best out-of-sample model.
statements.explanation: The lowest training error may occur well after generalization begins to worsen.

statements.text: If training is stopped too early, the model may underﬁt.
statements.explanation: Insufficient training can leave useful structure unlearned.

ML-D9G6Q3.subject: ML

ML-D10G1Q1.scenario: A systematic equity team ﬁnds that next-day returns change approximately in proportion to a small set of standardized factors. The PM wants a dependable baseline that can be retrained frequently and asks whether the team should begin with a deep tree instead of a linear model simply because the tree is more ﬂexible.

statements.text: A linear model is a reasonable starting point when the relevant relationship is approximately linear.
statements.explanation: The model structure matches the observed proportional relationship and provides a useful baseline.

statements.text: A more ﬂexible learner must have lower out-of-sample error because it can represent more functions.
statements.explanation: Additional ﬂexibility can ﬁt noise and does not guarantee better generalization.

statements.text: A simple model may outperform a complex model when the sample is limited or noisy.
statements.explanation: Lower variance can make a simpler learner more reliable under limited information.

statements.text: Comparing candidates on representative validation data is preferable to choosing solely from their theoretical ﬂexibility.
statements.explanation: Validation evidence tests how the tradeoff behaves on unseen observations.

statements.text: Standardizing the factors automatically makes every relationship linear.
statements.explanation: Scaling changes feature units, not the underlying functional form.

ML-D10G1Q1.subject: ML

ML-D10G1Q2.scenario: A commodity desk observes that returns rise only when momentum and inventory conditions jointly cross certain thresholds. The head researcher asks whether a straight-line model or a decision tree is better aligned with this structure, while requiring the recommendation to be supported out of sample. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: A decision tree can represent threshold-based interactions without the analyst explicitly specifying each interaction.
statements.explanation: Successive splits can encode conditional threshold relationships.

statements.text: A basic linear model with only additive raw features naturally reproduces every possible threshold interaction.
statements.explanation: An additive linear form does not automatically capture arbitrary thresholds or interactions.

statements.text: Feature engineering could allow a linear model to represent some nonlinear or interaction effects.
statements.explanation: Transformed and interaction features can expand what a linear model represents.

statements.text: The apparent threshold structure proves that the deepest possible tree is the best choice.
statements.explanation: Unrestricted depth can overﬁt sample-speciﬁc thresholds.

statements.text: Time-aware validation can help determine whether the threshold behavior persists beyond the training period.
statements.explanation: Later validation periods test whether the observed structure generalizes through time.

ML-D10G1Q2.subject: ML

ML-D10G1Q3.scenario: A cross-sectional strategy has thousands of highly correlated indicators but only two years of monthly observations. A client asks the team to use the most complex available ensemble because “more inputs require a more powerful model,” while the risk officer is concerned about unstable estimates. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: A large feature count does not by itself justify selecting the most complex learner.
statements.explanation: Model choice depends on usable information and constraints, not input count alone.

statements.text: Limited observations relative to model ﬂexibility can increase overﬁtting risk.
statements.explanation: A ﬂexible learner can discover many accidental patterns in a small sample.

statements.text: A constrained model or reduced feature set may be a defensible candidate.
statements.explanation: Reducing effective complexity may improve stability and generalization.

statements.text: Correlated indicators guarantee that an ensemble will produce independent errors among its members.
statements.explanation: Shared correlated inputs can cause learners to make similar errors.

statements.text: Model selection should consider sample size, redundancy, stability, and the intended prediction task together.
statements.explanation: These characteristics jointly determine whether a model is suitable. G2: Accuracy vs. Interpretability Tradeoffs

ML-D10G1Q3.subject: ML

ML-D10G2Q1.scenario: A bank uses a model to approve leverage limits for trading clients. An ensemble improves validation accuracy slightly over a linear model, but the compliance officer must explain adverse decisions and asks whether the accuracy gain should settle the choice.

statements.text: The ensemble’s higher validation accuracy is relevant but need not be the only selection criterion.
statements.explanation: Deployment decisions can include compliance, operational, and predictive objectives.

statements.text: A linear model may be preferred if its explanations satisfy an important governance requirement at an acceptable performance cost.
statements.explanation: A small accuracy sacriﬁce may be justiﬁed by a material explanation requirement.

statements.text: Interpretability matters only when two models have exactly equal predictive performance.
statements.explanation: Interpretability can be a binding constraint even when performance differs.

statements.text: Documenting the performance–interpretability tradeoff can support a defensible model decision.
statements.explanation: Explicit evidence makes the rationale and accepted compromise reviewable.

statements.text: Calling a model interpretable guarantees that its inputs are appropriate and free of leakage.
statements.explanation: Transparency does not validate the data or experimental design.

ML-D10G2Q1.subject: ML

ML-D10G2Q2.scenario: A hedge fund develops an internal signal used only to rank liquid stocks, and no individual client decision depends directly on the output. The PM favors a less transparent bagged-tree model because it produces a meaningful and stable out-of-sample improvement, while researchers still need to monitor it. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: The absence of a client-facing explanation requirement may reduce, but not eliminate, the value of interpretability.
statements.explanation: Research, debugging, risk, and oversight still beneﬁt from understanding behavior.

statements.text: A less interpretable model can be a reasonable choice when its beneﬁt is material and adequate controls exist.
statements.explanation: The acceptable balance depends on objectives, constraints, and controls.

statements.text: Internal use means the team need not understand inputs, failure modes, or regime sensitivity.
statements.explanation: Internal models can still create ﬁnancial and operational risk.

statements.text: Monitoring out-of-sample performance remains important regardless of model transparency.
statements.explanation: Live reliability cannot be inferred from transparency alone.

statements.text: Interpretability and accuracy are always perfectly opposed, so improving one must reduce the other.
statements.explanation: Some models can improve one dimension without necessarily harming the other.

ML-D10G2Q2.subject: ML

ML-D10G2Q3.scenario: A pension fund compares a shallow decision tree with a much deeper tree for a tactical allocation model. The deeper tree has a tiny validation advantage, but its recommendations change through many narrow rules that the investment committee cannot reliably review.

statements.text: The shallow tree’s decision path may be easier for the committee to inspect.
statements.explanation: Fewer splits generally produce a more compact explanation.

statements.text: The deeper tree should automatically be selected because any validation improvement dominates governance concerns.
statements.explanation: A negligible gain may not justify added complexity and oversight cost.

statements.text: The small performance difference should be evaluated for statistical and practical signiﬁcance.
statements.explanation: Sampling variation can make a tiny observed difference meaningless.

statements.text: Stability across multiple time splits could inform whether the deeper tree’s advantage is credible.
statements.explanation: Repeated evidence helps distinguish a durable gain from a lucky split.

statements.text: Choosing the shallow tree necessarily means abandoning all nonlinear relationships.
statements.explanation: Even a shallow tree can represent thresholds and limited interactions. G3: Training Time vs. Inference Time

ML-D10G2Q3.subject: ML

ML-D10G3Q1.scenario: You are selecting a model for a real-time trading system. The Head of Trading prioritizes speed, while a data scientist advocates for a complex ensemble.

statements.text: Inference time is more important than training time.
statements.explanation: Real-time systems require fast inference.

statements.text: KNN is often unsuitable due to latency.
statements.explanation: KNN is slow at inference.

statements.text: Linear models are often preferred for speed.
statements.explanation: Linear models are efficient.

statements.text: More complex models are always better.
statements.explanation: Tradeoffs exist.

statements.text: Model choice depends on system constraints.
statements.explanation: Context determines choice.

ML-D10G3Q1.subject: ML

ML-D10G3Q2.scenario: An asset manager retrains a weekly allocation model overnight and produces one set of portfolio weights before Monday’s open. The research director rejects a candidate because it takes 40 minutes to train, even though prediction takes milliseconds and the overnight window is four hours. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: The training time ﬁts within the stated retraining window.
statements.explanation: Forty minutes is below the available four-hour budget.

statements.text: Millisecond inference may be sufficient for a model that predicts only once per week.
statements.explanation: This use case has no stated need for high-frequency predictions.

statements.text: Training time and inference time should be evaluated against the workﬂow in which each cost occurs.
statements.explanation: Different operational schedules place different values on the two costs.

statements.text: A model that trains more slowly must also make predictions more slowly.
statements.explanation: Training and prediction have different computational patterns across learners.

statements.text: Rejecting the model solely because another model trains in one minute ignores whether the difference affects the deployment objective.
statements.explanation: A cost difference matters only insofar as it affects relevant constraints or resources.

ML-D10G3Q2.subject: ML

ML-D10G3Q3.scenario: A research platform serves thousands of interactive what-if requests against a ﬁxed model each day but retrains only at month-end. An analyst proposes KNN because ﬁtting mostly stores the data, while the platform owner is worried about response time and memory growth.

statements.text: KNN’s light ﬁtting procedure shifts substantial computation to prediction time.
statements.explanation: Neighbor search occurs when a new query is evaluated.

statements.text: KNN inference can become more expensive as the stored training set grows.
statements.explanation: More stored observations generally mean more distance computations absent special indexing.

statements.text: A ﬁtted linear model can often answer each request without scanning the full training set.
statements.explanation: Prediction typically uses the learned coefficient vector rather than all training rows.

statements.text: Because monthly retraining is infrequent, inference cost is irrelevant.
statements.explanation: Frequent serving can make inference the dominant operational cost.

statements.text: Expected request volume and memory constraints should be included in the model comparison.
statements.explanation: A deployable choice must meet throughput and resource requirements. G4: Sensitivity to Noise and Data Quality

ML-D10G3Q3.subject: ML

ML-D10G4Q1.group_title: Sensitivity to Noise and Data Quality
ML-D10G4Q1.scenario: A return-prediction dataset contains a few extreme target values caused by bad price adjustments. The PM notes that a linear regression ﬁt changes sharply when these rows are included and asks whether the resulting model should be trusted.

statements.text: Extreme target errors can strongly inﬂuence a least-squares ﬁt because large residuals are squared.
statements.explanation: Squared loss gives unusually large residuals disproportionate weight.

statements.text: Investigating and correcting conﬁrmed data errors is preferable to selecting a model solely to accommodate them.
statements.explanation: Data quality problems should be addressed at their source when possible.
