statements.text: Removing every economically extreme observation is automatically valid because outliers are always mistakes.
statements.explanation: Genuine market extremes may be informative and should not be discarded automatically.

statements.text: Comparing results with and without suspect rows can reveal sensitivity.
statements.explanation: Sensitivity analysis shows whether a small set of rows drives the conclusion.

statements.text: A good validation score guarantees that the underlying records are correctly adjusted.
statements.explanation: Aggregate performance cannot certify record-level data integrity.

ML-D10G4Q1.subject: ML

ML-D10G4Q2.group_title: Sensitivity to Noise and Data Quality
ML-D10G4Q2.scenario: A KNN strategy uses volatility, volume, and momentum features measured on very different scales. The head quant ﬁnds that small measurement noise in the high-magnitude volume feature changes which observations are selected as neighbors.

statements.text: Distance-based KNN can be sensitive to feature scale.
statements.explanation: Distance calculations reﬂect numerical magnitudes unless features are treated appropriately.

statements.text: Appropriate scaling can prevent one feature from dominating distance merely because of its units.
statements.explanation: Comparable scales make distance contributions less dependent on units.

statements.text: Scaling guarantees that noisy features become useful predictors.
statements.explanation: Scaling changes magnitude, not information content or measurement validity.

statements.text: Increasing k may reduce sensitivity to a single mislabeled or noisy neighbor, although excessive smoothing can add bias.
statements.explanation: Averaging more neighbors can dampen isolated noise but may erase local structure.

statements.text: Feature quality is irrelevant to KNN because it has no learned coefficients.
statements.explanation: Neighbor selection depends directly on the quality of the feature representation.

ML-D10G4Q2.subject: ML

ML-D10G4Q3.group_title: Sensitivity to Noise and Data Quality
ML-D10G4Q3.scenario: A single deep decision tree produces very different trading rules after a few training observations are corrected. The risk officer proposes a bagged ensemble and better data controls, but a researcher claims bagging makes clean data unnecessary. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Deep trees can be unstable because small data changes may alter early splits and downstream branches.
statements.explanation: A changed split can restructure much of a tree.

statements.text: Bagging can reduce variance by averaging predictions from multiple resampled trees.
statements.explanation: Aggregation can smooth sample-speciﬁc variation among members.

statements.text: Bagging guarantees immunity to systematic errors present throughout the dataset.
statements.explanation: Shared bias or corrupted inputs can affect every learner.

statements.text: Correcting upstream data defects can improve both single models and ensembles.
statements.explanation: Better inputs address a cause that aggregation alone cannot remove.

statements.text: Robustness should be assessed using plausible perturbations rather than assumed from the algorithm’s name.
statements.explanation: Empirical stress tests are needed to establish stability for the actual task. G5: Data Size vs. Model Complexity

ML-D10G4Q3.subject: ML

ML-D10G5Q1.scenario: A new crypto strategy has only 180 daily observations and 60 candidate indicators. The PM asks for a fully grown decision tree because it ﬁts the training period perfectly, while the analyst warns that the sample cannot support so many adaptive choices. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Perfect training ﬁt is weak evidence of generalization in this small-sample setting.
statements.explanation: A ﬂexible model can memorize a small dataset.

statements.text: A fully grown tree can partition the limited observations into highly speciﬁc leaves.
statements.explanation: Fine partitions may describe individual observations rather than recurring structure.

statements.text: Restricting depth or minimum leaf size may reduce overﬁtting risk.
statements.explanation: These controls limit effective model capacity.

statements.text: Adding more candidate indicators always reduces the amount of data required.
statements.explanation: More features can enlarge the search space and increase data requirements.

statements.text: Later out-of-sample observations are needed to evaluate whether the learned rules persist.
statements.explanation: Generalization must be tested beyond the observations used to construct the rules.

ML-D10G5Q1.subject: ML

ML-D10G5Q2.scenario: An equity desk expands from 5,000 to 5 million clean training examples and wants to reconsider models previously rejected for high variance. The engineering lead also notes that KNN would have to retain the enlarged dataset for prediction. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: More representative observations can make ﬁtting a ﬂexible model more reliable.
statements.explanation: More examples can help distinguish stable patterns from sampling noise.

statements.text: A larger dataset eliminates the need to control model complexity.
statements.explanation: Flexible models can still overﬁt, and data can contain noise or mismatch.

statements.text: KNN storage and naive inference costs can grow with the training set.
statements.explanation: KNN generally stores observations and compares queries against them.

statements.text: Scaling constraints may change which model is practical even when predictive accuracy improves.
statements.explanation: Memory, training, and serving costs are part of practical selection.

statements.text: The value of the additional rows depends on their relevance to the deployment distribution.
statements.explanation: Irrelevant or stale data may not improve current performance.

ML-D10G5Q2.subject: ML

ML-D10G5Q3.scenario: A global macro team pools decades of daily data to train a complex ensemble. The CIO argues that the raw row count is large enough, but many observations come from market structures that no longer exist and only a small fraction represents the current regime.

statements.text: Raw dataset size can overstate the amount of information relevant to current deployment.
statements.explanation: Effective sample relevance matters in addition to total count.

statements.text: More historical rows guarantee lower out-of-sample error in the current regime.
statements.explanation: Distribution shift can make additional history misleading.

statements.text: A complex model may learn obsolete relationships if regime differences are not addressed.
statements.explanation: Flexibility allows the learner to exploit patterns that may no longer operate.

statements.text: Time-based evaluation can help reveal whether performance transfers to more recent periods.
statements.explanation: Later evaluation periods better approximate the intended use.

statements.text: A simpler model may be competitive if it relies on fewer, more stable relationships.
statements.explanation: Reduced dependence on fragile structure can improve robustness. G6: Real-Time Constraints in Trading Systems

ML-D10G5Q3.subject: ML

ML-D10G6Q1.scenario: A market-making system must update quotes within 200 microseconds after receiving market data. A candidate ensemble improves offline error by 0.2% but exceeds the end-to-end latency budget during peak load, and the Head of Trading asks whether the gain justiﬁes deployment. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: A model that violates the latency budget may be unusable despite better offline error.
statements.explanation: Predictions that arrive too late cannot support the required decision.

statements.text: End-to-end testing under peak load is more relevant than timing one prediction in isolation.
statements.explanation: Production latency includes contention, tails, and surrounding system work.

statements.text: The ensemble should be deployed because predictive accuracy always dominates execution speed.
statements.explanation: Late decisions can erase or reverse the value of a small accuracy gain.

statements.text: A faster model with slightly worse prediction error could produce better realized trading outcomes.
statements.explanation: Timely execution can matter more than a modest offline improvement.

statements.text: Feature computation and system overhead should be included in the latency assessment.
statements.explanation: Model inference is only one component of the full response time.

ML-D10G6Q1.subject: ML

ML-D10G6Q2.scenario: A daily rebalancing strategy generates orders once after the close and has a 30-minute computation window. A junior engineer insists that only models suitable for high-frequency trading should be considered because all trading systems are real time.

statements.text: The daily strategy has a materially different latency requirement from a market-making system.
statements.explanation: Its decisions occur on a much slower schedule.

statements.text: A slower model can be acceptable if it completes reliably within the decision window.
statements.explanation: Meeting the actual deadline is more important than minimizing latency without purpose.

statements.text: High-frequency suitability is a universal requirement for any model used in ﬁnance.
statements.explanation: Model constraints depend on the strategy’s holding period and operating design.

statements.text: The team may reasonably prioritize robustness or interpretability over microsecond inference in this workﬂow.
statements.explanation: The generous time budget permits other objectives to carry more weight.

statements.text: Operational deadlines still matter even when the strategy is not high frequency.
statements.explanation: Missing the rebalance window could still disrupt execution.

ML-D10G6Q2.subject: ML

ML-D10G6Q3.scenario: A low-latency desk considers moving from a linear model to KNN as its historical dataset grows each day. The proposed system must handle bursts of simultaneous predictions, and the engineering manager asks the research team to account for tail latency rather than average latency alone.

statements.text: Naive KNN prediction can slow as the stored dataset grows.
statements.explanation: Each query may require distances to an increasing number of observations.

statements.text: Burst traffic can make high-percentile latency more important than a low average.
statements.explanation: Averages can hide rare delays that violate trading deadlines.

statements.text: The absence of a costly ﬁtting phase makes KNN automatically suitable for low-latency serving.
statements.explanation: KNN defers much of its computational burden to inference.

statements.text: Limiting the reference set could improve speed but may change predictive behavior.
statements.explanation: Fewer comparisons reduce work but can exclude relevant neighbors.

statements.text: The model comparison should include throughput, memory, and latency under representative load.
statements.explanation: These measures determine whether the model can operate within the system constraints. G7: Robustness and Stability in Production

ML-D10G6Q3.subject: ML

ML-D10G7Q1.scenario: A live forecasting model performed well during calm markets but its errors rise sharply when volatility increases. The risk committee asks whether strong average backtest performance is enough to keep the model active without changes. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Average performance can conceal failure in economically important regimes.
statements.explanation: Poor stressed-period behavior may be hidden by many calm observations.

statements.text: Evaluating results by volatility regime can reveal conditional weaknesses.
statements.explanation: Segmented evaluation tests whether performance depends on market state.

statements.text: Historical success guarantees that the relationship will remain stable in production.
statements.explanation: Markets and data-generating relationships can change.

statements.text: Monitoring can support thresholds for review, fallback, or retraining when behavior deteriorates.
statements.explanation: Deﬁned responses make degradation actionable rather than merely observable.

statements.text: A simpler fallback model may be valuable even if it is not the top performer in normal conditions.
statements.explanation: Operational resilience may favor a dependable alternative during failures.

ML-D10G7Q1.subject: ML

ML-D10G7Q2.scenario: A deep tree and a bagged-tree ensemble have similar average validation error. Across nearby time windows and small input perturbations, the single tree’s predictions vary much more, while the ensemble remains relatively consistent; the production owner values predictable exposures.

statements.text: The ensemble’s lower sensitivity may be relevant even when average error is similar.
statements.explanation: Prediction variability can affect turnover, exposure, and operational conﬁdence.

statements.text: Bagging can reduce variance by averaging unstable component predictions.
statements.explanation: Aggregation reduces the inﬂuence of sample-speciﬁc tree behavior.

statements.text: Similar average error proves that the two models create identical trading risk.
statements.explanation: Models with equal average error can differ in tails, turnover, and sensitivity.

statements.text: Small-perturbation tests can provide evidence about local model stability.
statements.explanation: Such tests measure whether modest changes cause disproportionate output changes.

statements.text: Stability considerations may justify selecting the ensemble for production.
statements.explanation: Production suitability includes reliability beyond mean accuracy.

ML-D10G7Q2.subject: ML

ML-D10G7Q3.scenario: A factor model is retrained monthly, and the selected features and coefficients change dramatically each time even though headline validation scores remain similar. The model-risk lead asks whether this instability should be investigated before clients rely on the resulting allocations.

statements.text: Similar validation scores do not rule out unstable model behavior.
statements.explanation: Different models can achieve similar scores while producing materially different outputs.

statements.text: Large month-to-month changes may indicate correlated features, limited data, or regime sensitivity.
statements.explanation: Each condition can cause ﬁtted relationships to shift across samples.

statements.text: Comparing portfolio turnover and exposure changes can reveal practical consequences of instability.
statements.explanation: Allocation changes translate statistical instability into costs and risk.

statements.text: Retraining more often necessarily makes the model more stable.
statements.explanation: More frequent ﬁtting may amplify sensitivity to short-term sample changes.

statements.text: Stability analysis should consider both predictions and downstream decisions.
statements.explanation: Production impact depends on what the system does with the predictions. G8: Comparative Model Reasoning

ML-D10G7Q3.subject: ML

ML-D10G8Q1.scenario: A PM must choose among linear regression, KNN, and a decision tree for a medium-sized return-prediction dataset. The relationship may contain thresholds, inference must be fast, and the investment committee wants a model it can inspect. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: Linear regression offers fast inference and transparent coefficients but may miss unengineered threshold effects.
statements.explanation: Its strengths and limitations align with the stated tradeoff.

statements.text: A decision tree can represent thresholds and provide inspectable rules, subject to complexity limits.
statements.explanation: Splits capture thresholds, while pruning or depth limits can aid review and generalization.

statements.text: KNN naturally provides a compact global equation explaining all predictions.
statements.explanation: KNN predictions depend on local stored examples rather than one compact ﬁtted equation.

statements.text: No learner is universally best across the stated objectives.
statements.explanation: The models offer different balances of structure, speed, and interpretability.

statements.text: Representative validation and operational tests should inform the ﬁnal choice.
statements.explanation: Both predictive and deployment evidence are needed.

ML-D10G8Q1.subject: ML

ML-D10G8Q2.scenario: A research team compares three learners on a nonlinear signal. KNN performs best on a small validation set, a tree is close behind, and a linear model is slightly worse but far more stable across time splits. The CIO asks the team to name the winner immediately. The team asks you to identify the ﬂawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.text: The single validation ranking may be uncertain because the validation set is small.
statements.explanation: Sampling variation can materially affect results from a small evaluation set.

statements.text: Stability across time splits is relevant evidence for a trading model.
statements.explanation: Market relationships and samples vary through time.

statements.text: KNN must be selected because the lowest observed error always identiﬁes the true best model.
statements.explanation: An observed lead may reﬂect noise and ignores other constraints.

statements.text: The linear model’s stability may justify selection if the small accuracy difference is unreliable or operationally unimportant.
statements.explanation: Reliability can outweigh a marginal, uncertain improvement.

statements.text: The team should compare the models using consistent splits and metrics.
statements.explanation: Consistency is necessary for a fair comparison.

ML-D10G8Q2.subject: ML

ML-D10G8Q3.scenario: A trading desk summarizes its options as follows: a linear model is fast and stable but underﬁts; a deep tree ﬁts nonlinearities but is unstable; and KNN is accurate offline but too slow with the full dataset. The research director asks for a recommendation that improves the system rather than declaring one algorithm inherently superior.

statements.text: Feature engineering may improve the linear model while retaining fast inference.
statements.explanation: Appropriate transformations can capture additional structure without changing the basic serving pattern.

statements.text: Restricting tree depth or using a bagged-tree ensemble may address some variance concerns.
statements.explanation: Complexity controls or averaging can reduce sensitivity, though they introduce their own tradeoffs.

statements.text: Reducing or restructuring KNN’s reference data may improve latency but requires re-evaluating accuracy.
statements.explanation: Computational savings can alter neighbor quality and must be validated.

statements.text: Because each model has a weakness, none can be deployed under any circumstances.
statements.explanation: Practical model selection manages tradeoffs rather than requiring perfection.

statements.text: The best choice is the one that achieves an acceptable balance under the desk’s measured constraints.
statements.explanation: Suitability is conditional on predictive, operational, and governance requirements.

ML-D10G8Q3.subject: ML

QF-D1G1Q1.scenario: A portfolio manager buys a stock at $50. At the end of the ﬁrst month, it closes at $55; at the end of the second month, it closes at $52.25. Ignoring dividends and trading costs, the manager asks a junior analyst to explain the two monthly returns and the return over the full holding period.

statements.text: The ﬁrst-month return is 10%.
statements.explanation: The ﬁrst-month return is ($55 - $50) / $50 = 10%.

statements.text: The second-month return is -5%, measured relative to the $55 value at the beginning of that month.
statements.explanation: The second-month return is ($52.25 - $55) / $55 = -5%.

statements.text: The two-month cumulative return is 5% because the monthly returns sum to 5%.
statements.explanation: Linked returns compound: (1.10)(0.95) - 1 = 4.5%, not 5%.

statements.text: One dollar invested at the beginning would not be worth $1.045 at the end.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. A cumulative return of 4.5% turns $1.00 into $1.045.

statements.text: The $2.25 increase in price represents the same percentage return regardless of the stock's initial purchase price.
statements.explanation: Percentage return depends on the price used as the starting value.

QF-D1G1Q1.subject: QF

QF-D1G1Q2.scenario: An investment committee reviews a fund that returned 8% in the ﬁrst quarter and -6% in the second quarter. The chair wants a single ﬁrst-half performance number and asks whether simply reporting 2% would be accurate. Assume there were no external cash ﬂows or fees.

statements.text: The ﬁrst-half cumulative return is found by multiplying 1.08 by 0.94 and subtracting 1.
statements.explanation: Consecutive periodic returns are linked multiplicatively.

statements.text: The fund's ﬁrst-half cumulative return is 1.52%.
Adding the quarterly returns gives the exact cumulative return whenever the periods are consecutive.
statements.explanation: Adding returns ignores compounding and is generally only an approximation.

statements.text: If the fund began with $10 million, it ended the half-year with $10.152 million.
statements.explanation: $10 million × 1.0152 = $10.152 million.

statements.text: The second-quarter dollar loss is not computed using the portfolio value after the ﬁrst-quarter gain.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. The -6% return applies to the $10.8 million value entering the second quarter.

QF-D1G1Q2.subject: QF

QF-D1G1Q3.scenario: A family office compares a stock that rose from $80 to $88 with another that rose from $20 to $24. A client calls the ﬁrst stock the better performer because its price increased by more dollars. You are asked to evaluate that claim, ignoring dividends and costs.

statements.text: A reviewer would be wrong to accept the claim that the ﬁrst stock earned a 10% return.
statements.explanation: The underlying claim is correct and should be accepted. ($88 - $80) / $80 = 10%.

statements.text: The second stock earned a 20% return.
The ﬁrst stock had the larger dollar price change per share.
statements.explanation: The ﬁrst rose $8 per share, while the second rose $4 per share.

statements.text: The ﬁrst stock outperformed the second on a percentage-return basis.
statements.explanation: The second stock's 20% return exceeds the ﬁrst stock's 10% return.

statements.text: If equal dollar amounts had been invested in the two stocks, the second investment would not have produced the larger dollar proﬁt.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. With equal starting capital, the higher percentage return produces the larger dollar proﬁt. G2: Compounding and Geometric Growth

QF-D1G1Q3.subject: QF

QF-D1G2Q1.scenario: A pension consultant reports that a private investment grew from $100 million to $121 million over two years. The pension board wants to compare the investment with alternatives quoted using annual growth rates and asks for the investment's CAGR. Assume there were no interim cash ﬂows.

statements.text: The investment's total two-year return is 21%.
statements.explanation: $121 million / $100 million - 1 = 21%.

statements.text: Its CAGR is not 10% per year.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. ($121 / $100)^(1/2) - 1 = 10%.

statements.text: A 10.5% annual simple average is the realized annual compound growth rate.
statements.explanation: Dividing the 21% total return by two ignores compounding and does not produce CAGR.

statements.text: Compounding a 10% annual return for two years produces a 21% cumulative return.
CAGR describes the constant annual rate that would connect the beginning and ending values.
statements.explanation: CAGR is the constant compounded rate consistent with the two endpoint values.

QF-D1G2Q1.subject: QF

QF-D1G2Q2.scenario: A retirement-plan sponsor is comparing two long-term savings options. One is expected to earn 8% annually before a 1% annual fee, while the other is expected to earn 7.25% annually with no fee. The sponsor asks why a seemingly small annual fee matters over a 30-year horizon; assume each quoted net or gross rate compounds annually and ignore taxes.

statements.text: The ﬁrst option's assumed net annual growth rate is not 7% under the simpliﬁed fee assumption.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Under the stated simpliﬁcation, 8% gross less a 1% annual fee gives 7% net.

statements.text: At a 7% net rate, $1 grows to approximately $7.61 over 30 years.
statements.explanation: (1.07)^30 is approximately 7.61.

statements.text: At a 7.25% rate, $1 grows to more than it does at a 7% rate over the same horizon.
statements.explanation: With the same starting wealth and horizon, the higher positive compound rate produces greater terminal wealth.

statements.text: The 0.25 percentage-point difference can be evaluated by multiplying 0.25% by 30 to obtain the exact terminal-wealth difference.
statements.explanation: The terminal-wealth difference depends on compounding, not simple multiplication of the rate gap by time.

statements.text: Repeated compounding cannot make a small annual return difference economically meaningful over a long horizon.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Each year's difference affects the base on which later returns compound.

QF-D1G2Q2.subject: QF

QF-D1G2Q3.scenario: A wealth manager uses the Rule of 72 to give a client a quick sense of long-horizon growth. The client is considering an account expected to earn 6% annually and wants to know how long it might take to double, while acknowledging that the return is not guaranteed.

statements.text: The Rule of 72 estimates a doubling time of about 12 years at 6% annual growth.
statements.explanation: 72 / 6 gives an approximate doubling time of 12 years.

statements.text: The estimate is obtained by dividing 72 by the annual percentage return.
statements.explanation: That calculation is the standard Rule of 72 approximation.

statements.text: The Rule of 72 guarantees the account will double in the estimated period.
statements.explanation: It is an approximation based on an assumed rate, not a performance guarantee.

statements.text: The exact doubling time at a constant 6% annual compound rate is not slightly less than 12 years.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. ln(2) / ln(1.06) is approximately 11.9 years.

statements.text: If the net return fell to 4%, the Rule of 72 would imply a longer doubling time.
statements.explanation: 72 / 4 is about 18 years, which is longer than 12 years. G3: Arithmetic vs. Geometric Average Returns

QF-D1G2Q3.subject: QF

QF-D1G3Q1.scenario: A hedge-fund analyst reports annual returns of +30% and -20% and tells the investment committee that the fund's average return was 5% per year. The committee asks whether that ﬁgure describes the fund's realized compound growth. Assume no cash ﬂows or fees.

statements.text: The arithmetic average return is 5%.
The two-year cumulative return is not 4%.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. (1.30)(0.80) - 1 = 4%.

statements.text: The geometric average return is not approximately 1.98% per year.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. The geometric average is sqrt(1.04) - 1, approximately 1.98%.

statements.text: Investing $100 at the beginning would produce $110.25 after two years.
statements.explanation: The terminal value is $100 × 1.30 × 0.80 = $104.

statements.text: The arithmetic average overstates the annualized compound growth achieved over these two years.
statements.explanation: The 5% arithmetic mean exceeds the approximately 1.98% geometric mean.

QF-D1G3Q1.subject: QF

QF-D1G3Q2.scenario: A quant researcher is using historical annual returns for two different tasks: estimating a representative one-year expected return and describing the constant annual rate actually earned across the full sample. The research lead asks the analyst to choose the averaging method appropriate to each task.

statements.text: The arithmetic mean is generally more relevant for estimating the average outcome of a single future period from a historical sample.
statements.explanation: The arithmetic mean summarizes the average one-period observation.

statements.text: The geometric mean is appropriate for describing the constant compound rate linking beginning wealth to ending wealth over multiple periods.
statements.explanation: The geometric mean reﬂects realized multi-period compounding.

statements.text: The geometric mean can be calculated by adding periodic returns and dividing by the number of periods.
statements.explanation: The geometric mean is based on multiplying growth factors and taking the appropriate root.

statements.text: When periodic returns vary and compound wealth remains positive, the geometric mean cannot exceed the arithmetic mean.
statements.explanation: Return variability creates a gap in which the geometric mean is less than or equal to the arithmetic mean.

statements.text: The arithmetic and geometric means are always identical when the sample contains both positive and negative returns.
statements.explanation: They are equal only when the periodic returns are identical, not merely because signs differ.

QF-D1G3Q2.subject: QF

QF-D1G3Q3.scenario: An allocator compares two hypothetical strategies over two years. Strategy A earns +10% in each year; Strategy B earns +40% in the ﬁrst year and -20% in the second. Both have an arithmetic average return of 10%, and the allocator wants to know whether they create the same terminal wealth from a $100 investment.

statements.text: A reviewer would be wrong to accept the claim that strategy A ends with $121.
statements.explanation: The underlying claim is correct and should be accepted. $100 × 1.10 × 1.10 = $121.

statements.text: A reviewer would be wrong to accept the claim that strategy B ends with $112.
statements.explanation: The underlying claim is correct and should be accepted. $100 × 1.40 × 0.80 = $112.

statements.text: Both strategies have the same geometric average because their arithmetic averages are equal.
statements.explanation: Strategy A's geometric average is 10%, while Strategy B's is sqrt(1.12) - 1, approximately 5.83%.

statements.text: Strategy B's greater return variability creates volatility drag relative to its arithmetic average.
statements.explanation: The dispersion in Strategy B's returns lowers its compound growth relative to its 10% arithmetic mean.

statements.text: Strategy A has a 10% geometric average return.
statements.explanation: Identical 10% returns in both years produce a 10% geometric mean. G4: Annualization and Time-Scale Conversion

QF-D1G3Q3.subject: QF

QF-D1G4Q1.scenario: An asset manager reports a strategy that earned 1% in each of the past 12 months. A client asks for its annual return, while the risk team separately reports monthly volatility of 3%. Assume monthly returns compound and, for volatility scaling, monthly returns are independent with stable variance.

statements.text: The compounded annual return is approximately 12.68%.
statements.explanation: (1.01)^12 - 1 is approximately 12.68%.

statements.text: Multiplying 1% by 12 gives the exact compounded annual return.
statements.explanation: 12% is a simple approximation that omits monthly compounding.

statements.text: The annualized volatility is approximately 10.39%.
statements.explanation: 3% × sqrt(12) is approximately 10.39%.

statements.text: Monthly volatility is annualized by multiplying by 12.
statements.explanation: Under the stated assumptions, volatility scales with the square root of time.

statements.text: Return and volatility use different common annualization rules in this scenario.
statements.explanation: Returns compound across periods, while volatility is scaled by sqrt(12) under the given assumptions.

QF-D1G4Q1.subject: QF

QF-D1G4Q2.scenario: A trading desk observes a mean daily strategy return of 0.04% and daily volatility of 1.2%. The desk uses 252 trading days per year and asks for annualized ﬁgures to compare with another strategy. Assume daily returns are independent and identically distributed for this simpliﬁed comparison.

statements.text: Multiplying the mean daily return by 252 gives an arithmetic annualized-return approximation of 10.08%.
Compounding 0.04% for 252 days gives an effective annual return of approximately 10.60%.
statements.explanation: (1.0004)^252 - 1 is approximately 10.60%.

statements.text: The annualized volatility is not approximately 19.05%.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. 1.2% × sqrt(252) is approximately 19.05%.

statements.text: Annualized volatility should be calculated as 1.2% × 252.
statements.explanation: Volatility scales with sqrt(252), not 252, under the stated assumptions.

statements.text: A reviewer would be wrong to accept the claim that the assumed number of trading days affects both reported annualized ﬁgures.
statements.explanation: The underlying claim is correct and should be accepted. Both calculations explicitly use the selected number of periods per year.

QF-D1G4Q2.subject: QF

QF-D1G4Q3.scenario: A risk committee receives a report comparing Strategy X's 1.5% monthly return with Strategy Y's 14% annual return. The report declares X superior because 1.5 is greater than 14 after converting both percentages to decimals incorrectly. The committee asks you to put the returns on a consistent basis; assume X earns 1.5% every month.

statements.text: The two quoted returns should not be converted to the same time horizon before comparison.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Valid comparison requires consistent units and horizons.

statements.text: Strategy X's effective annual return is approximately 19.56%.
statements.explanation: (1.015)^12 - 1 is approximately 19.56%.

statements.text: Multiplying 1.5% by 12 gives an exact effective annual return of 18%.
statements.explanation: 18% omits monthly compounding and is only a simple annualized approximation.

statements.text: Under the stated constant-return assumption, Strategy X has the higher annual return.
statements.explanation: Approximately 19.56% exceeds Strategy Y's 14% annual return.

statements.text: Comparing a monthly ﬁgure directly with an annual ﬁgure can lead to an invalid conclusion even when both are expressed as percentages.
statements.explanation: Percentage notation alone does not make the measurement periods comparable. G5: Portfolio Return Aggregation

QF-D1G4Q3.subject: QF

QF-D1G5Q1.scenario: A balanced fund begins the month with 60% invested in equities and 40% in bonds. During the month, equities return 10% and bonds return -5%. The portfolio manager wants the fund's return before fees and assumes there was no rebalancing or external cash ﬂow during the month.

statements.text: Equities contribute 6 percentage points to the portfolio return.
statements.explanation: 60% × 10% = a 6-percentage-point contribution.

statements.text: Bonds contribute -2 percentage points to the portfolio return.
statements.explanation: 40% × -5% = a -2-percentage-point contribution.

statements.text: The portfolio return is 5%, the simple average of the two asset returns.
statements.explanation: Asset returns must be weighted by portfolio allocations; the equal-weight average is not applicable.

statements.text: The portfolio return is not 4%.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. 6% - 2% = 4%.

statements.text: The equity return and its contribution to portfolio return are the same because equities had a positive return.
statements.explanation: The asset earned 10%, but its portfolio contribution was 6 percentage points due to its 60% weight.

QF-D1G5Q1.subject: QF

QF-D1G5Q2.scenario: A long-short equity fund begins the month 130% long Stock A and 30% short Stock B, leaving net exposure of 100% and gross exposure of 160%. During the month, Stock A rises 6% and Stock B rises 2%. Ignore ﬁnancing costs, fees, and rebalancing.

statements.text: Stock A contributes 7.8 percentage points to portfolio return.
statements.explanation: 1.30 × 6% = 7.8 percentage points.

statements.text: The short position contributes -0.6 percentage points because Stock B increased in value.
statements.explanation: The -0.30 weight multiplied by a +2% asset return contributes -0.6 percentage points.

statements.text: The portfolio return is not 7.2%.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. 7.8% - 0.6% = 7.2%.

statements.text: The fund's 100% net exposure means leverage has no effect on its return.
statements.explanation: Gross exposure is 160%, and the leveraged long and short positions both affect return and risk.

statements.text: If Stock B had instead fallen 2%, the short position would have contributed positively.
statements.explanation: A negative position weight multiplied by a negative asset return produces a positive contribution.

QF-D1G5Q2.subject: QF

QF-D1G5Q3.scenario: A tactical portfolio invests 120% of capital in a market ETF and ﬁnances the extra 20% by borrowing at 1% for the period. The ETF returns 10% during that period. The chief investment officer asks for the portfolio return before any other fees and wants the effect of leverage made explicit.

statements.text: The ETF position contributes 12 percentage points to portfolio return.
statements.explanation: A 120% weight multiplied by a 10% return contributes 12 percentage points.

statements.text: The borrowing cost reduces portfolio return by 0.2 percentage points.
statements.explanation: Borrowing 20% of capital at 1% costs 0.2% of portfolio capital.

statements.text: The resulting portfolio return is not 11.8%.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. 12% - 0.2% = 11.8%.

statements.text: Because the portfolio's net invested weight is 100%, its return must equal the ETF's 10% return.
statements.explanation: Borrowing creates leveraged exposure, so both the 120% asset position and ﬁnancing cost matter.

statements.text: If the ETF instead lost 10%, leverage would not magnify the loss before ﬁnancing costs.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. A 120% ETF position would contribute -12%, compared with - 10% without leverage, before borrowing cost. G6: Gross, Net, and Benchmark-Relative Performance

QF-D1G5Q3.subject: QF

QF-D1G6Q1.scenario: A systematic fund earns a 12% gross return for the year. Transaction costs equal 2% of beginning capital and the management fee equals 1% of beginning capital; for this question, subtract both directly from gross return. The fund's appropriate benchmark earns 8%, and the client asks whether the strategy added value after implementation costs and fees.

statements.text: The fund's net return is 9%.
statements.explanation: 12% - 2% - 1% = 9% under the stated simpliﬁcation.

statements.text: Its gross excess return over the benchmark is not 4 percentage points.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. 12% - 8% = 4 percentage points.

statements.text: Its net excess return over the benchmark is 1 percentage point.
statements.explanation: 9% - 8% = 1 percentage point.

statements.text: Because its gross return exceeded the benchmark, its net return must also exceed the benchmark regardless of costs.
statements.explanation: Sufficiently large costs and fees can eliminate or reverse gross outperformance.

statements.text: Reporting only the 12% gross return would overstate the return retained by the investor under these assumptions.
statements.explanation: The investor retains 9%, not the 12% pre-cost result.

QF-D1G6Q1.subject: QF

QF-D1G6Q2.scenario: A hedge fund earns 15% before fees on $100 million of beginning capital. Its agreement charges a 2% management fee on beginning capital and a 20% incentive fee on proﬁts remaining after the management fee; ignore high-water marks and other expenses. An investor asks the analyst to calculate the simpliﬁed net result.

statements.text: The management fee is not $2 million.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. 2% of $100 million is $2 million.

statements.text: Proﬁt remaining after the management fee is $13 million.
statements.explanation: The $15 million gross proﬁt is reduced to $13 million after the management fee.

statements.text: The incentive fee is $3 million because it is always 20% of gross proﬁt.
statements.explanation: Under the stated agreement, the incentive fee is 20% of $13 million, or $2.6 million.

statements.text: The investor's net proﬁt is not $10.4 million.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. $15 million - $2 million - $2.6 million = $10.4 million.

statements.text: The investor's net return is 10.4% under the stated assumptions.
statements.explanation: $10.4 million divided by $100 million of beginning capital is 10.4%.

QF-D1G6Q2.subject: QF

QF-D1G6Q3.scenario: A technology-focused long-only fund loses 6% during a market selloff, while its agreed technology-sector benchmark loses 10%. A client says the manager failed because the fund had a negative absolute return; the manager says the fund succeeded because it beat the benchmark. The oversight committee asks you to distinguish the two claims.

statements.text: The fund's absolute return is -6%.
statements.explanation: Absolute performance is the fund's own -6% return.

statements.text: The fund's benchmark-relative return is not +4 percentage points.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. -6% - (-10%) = +4 percentage points.

statements.text: The fund can have a negative absolute return and a positive relative return at the same time.
statements.explanation: Losing less than the benchmark creates positive relative performance despite an absolute loss.

statements.text: Outperforming the benchmark means every investor objective was necessarily achieved.
statements.explanation: An investor may also have capital-preservation, risk, liability, or absolute-return objectives.

statements.text: Replacing the technology benchmark with cash could materially change the assessment of relative performance.
statements.explanation: Excess return depends on the selected benchmark, so benchmark suitability matters. G7: Path Dependence and Return Sequencing

QF-D1G6Q3.subject: QF

QF-D1G7Q1.scenario: A portfolio manager reports that a strategy gained 50% in the ﬁrst year and lost 50% in the second year. She tells the investment committee that the average annual return was 0%, so the portfolio ﬁnished where it started. You are asked to assess that conclusion.

statements.text: The arithmetic average of the two annual returns is not 0%.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. The arithmetic mean of +50% and -50% is 0%.

statements.text: The portfolio ﬁnishes with the same value it started with.
statements.explanation: A portfolio starting at $100 rises to $150 and then falls to $75.

statements.text: A 50% loss requires a 100% gain to recover fully.
statements.explanation: A 100% gain is required to grow $75 back to $150.

statements.text: The geometric average return over the two years is not negative.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Terminal wealth is below starting wealth, so the compounded average is negative.

statements.text: The combination of gains and losses can produce terminal wealth below the starting value even when the arithmetic average return is 0%.
statements.explanation: Returns compound multiplicatively, and equal percentage gains and losses do not offset.

QF-D1G7Q1.subject: QF

QF-D1G7Q2.scenario: Two retirees each begin with $1 million and withdraw $100,000 at the end of each year. Portfolio A earns +20% in Year 1 and -20% in Year 2; Portfolio B earns -20% in Year 1 and +20% in Year 2. Their adviser claims the order cannot matter because both portfolios experience the same two returns. Ignore taxes and fees.

statements.text: Before withdrawals, the same two returns would not produce the same terminal wealth regardless of their order.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Without cash ﬂows, multiplication is commutative: (1.20)(0.80) produces the same result in either order.

statements.text: After the Year 1 return and withdrawal, Portfolio A has $1.1 million.
After both returns and both withdrawals, Portfolio A has $800,000.
After both returns and both withdrawals, Portfolio B has $740,000.
The withdrawal requirement creates sequence-of-returns risk even though the two portfolios have the same arithmetic and geometric average returns.
statements.explanation: Withdrawals change the capital exposed to later returns, making their order economically important.

QF-D1G7Q2.subject: QF

QF-D1G7Q3.scenario: A risk committee reviews a strategy that falls from a previous peak value of $100 million to $70 million and later recovers to $91 million. The portfolio manager says the subsequent 30% gain completely erased the earlier 30% drawdown. The committee asks you to verify the recovery mathematics.

statements.text: The decline from $100 million to $70 million is not a 30% drawdown.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. ($70 million - $100 million) / $100 million = -30%.

statements.text: A 30% gain on $70 million raises the portfolio to $91 million.
statements.explanation: $70 million × 1.30 = $91 million.

statements.text: A reviewer would be wrong to accept the claim that returning from $70 million to the prior $100 million peak requires approximately a 42.86% gain.
statements.explanation: The underlying claim is correct and should be accepted. $100 million / $70 million - 1 is approximately 42.86%.

statements.text: A loss of x% is always recovered by a gain of x%.
statements.explanation: After a loss, the recovery gain is applied to a smaller base and must therefore be larger.

statements.text: At $91 million, the portfolio remains 9% below its prior peak.
statements.explanation: ($91 million - $100 million) / $100 million = -9%.

QF-D1G7Q3.subject: QF

QF-D2G1Q1.scenario: A risk committee compares two market-neutral strategies that each earned an average monthly return of 1%. Strategy A returned 1% in every observed month, while Strategy B alternated between 5% and -3%; the chief risk officer asks whether their identical average returns imply identical risk.

statements.text: Strategy A has zero historical return variance over the stated sample.
statements.explanation: Every observed return for Strategy A equals its mean, so each deviation from the mean is zero.

statements.text: Strategy B has greater historical return dispersion than Strategy A.
statements.explanation: Strategy B's returns repeatedly deviate from the 1% mean, whereas Strategy A's do not.

statements.text: The two strategies must have the same standard deviation because their arithmetic average returns are equal.
statements.explanation: Equal means do not imply equal dispersion or standard deviation.

statements.text: Variance is expressed in squared-return units, while standard deviation is expressed in the same units as return.
statements.explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of variance and returns to the original return units.

statements.text: Based only on these observations, Strategy B provided a smoother realized return path than Strategy A.
statements.explanation: Strategy A's constant returns form the smoother observed path.

QF-D2G1Q1.subject: QF

QF-D2G1Q2.scenario: An asset allocator is choosing between Fund X, with a 12% expected annual return and 10% annual volatility, and Fund Y, with a 14% expected annual return and 24% annual volatility. The allocator's client wants growth but is concerned about year-to-year uncertainty and asks how to interpret the volatility estimates.

statements.text: Fund Y has the higher expected raw return.
statements.explanation: Fund Y's expected return is 14%, compared with 12% for Fund X.

statements.text: Fund Y's return outcomes are estimated to be more dispersed around its expected return.
statements.explanation: Its 24% standard deviation indicates greater estimated dispersion than Fund X's 10%.

statements.text: A 24% volatility estimate means Fund Y will lose exactly 24% in one out of every two years.
statements.explanation: Volatility is a dispersion measure, not a ﬁxed loss amount or frequency guarantee.

statements.text: Fund X's lower volatility guarantees it will never experience a large loss.
statements.explanation: Lower volatility does not eliminate tail events, estimation error, or the possibility of loss.

statements.text: Choosing Fund Y solely because of its 14% expected return would not ignore a material difference in estimated risk.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. The higher expected return is accompanied by substantially higher estimated volatility.

QF-D2G1Q2.subject: QF

QF-D2G1Q3.scenario: A quant team reviews a strategy whose ﬁrst 23 monthly returns were clustered tightly around 0.5%, but whose twenty- fourth return was -18%. The portfolio manager wants to omit the ﬁnal month as "unrepresentative" before presenting the strategy's risk statistics to an investment committee.

statements.text: Including the -18% month will not generally increase the estimated variance relative to a sample containing only the tightly clustered months.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. A return far from the rest of the sample creates a large deviation and generally raises measured dispersion.

statements.text: Squaring deviations in the variance calculation makes a large deviation inﬂuential.
statements.explanation: Squaring gives disproportionate weight to observations far from the mean.

statements.text: Removing the observation solely because it worsens the reported risk could create a misleading comparison.
statements.explanation: Selective exclusion can understate the risk investors actually faced.

statements.text: The extreme observation can affect standard deviation but cannot affect the sample's mean return.
statements.explanation: Every included observation affects the arithmetic mean as well as dispersion statistics.

statements.text: A risk review should investigate whether the observation is erroneous or reﬂects a genuine strategy exposure before deciding how to treat it.
statements.explanation: Data errors and genuine tail outcomes require different treatment, so the cause matters. G2: Downside Risk and Drawdown

QF-D2G1Q3.subject: QF

QF-D2G2Q1.scenario: A fund rises from a net asset value of $100 to $125, declines to $90, and later recovers to $110. The fund manager highlights the $10 gain from inception, but a prospective investor asks the risk team to describe the loss experienced from the fund's high-water mark.

statements.text: The decline from $125 to $90 is not a 28% drawdown.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. ($90 - $125) / $125 = -28%.

statements.text: The maximum drawdown over the stated path is not measured from the $125 peak to the $90 trough.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. That is the largest stated peak-to-subsequent-trough decline.

statements.text: Because the ending value of $110 exceeds the initial $100, the fund experienced no drawdown.
statements.explanation: Drawdown is measured relative to a prior peak, not only from inception to the ending value.

statements.text: Recovering from $90 to the prior $125 peak requires a gain of approximately 38.9%.
statements.explanation: $125 / $90 - 1 is approximately 38.9%.

statements.text: At the ending value of $110, the fund remains 12% below its prior peak.

QF-D2G2Q1.subject: QF

QF-D2G2Q2.scenario: A pension plan compares Strategy A, which experiences frequent small ﬂuctuations but never falls more than 6% from a prior peak, with Strategy B, which appears stable for years and then loses 30% before recovering. The investment committee has a 15% drawdown tolerance and asks whether ordinary volatility alone captures its concern.

statements.text: Strategy B violates the committee's stated drawdown tolerance during the observed loss.
statements.explanation: A 30% drawdown exceeds the stated 15% tolerance.

statements.text: A strategy can show low volatility for much of a sample yet still experience a severe drawdown.
statements.explanation: A rare large loss may follow a long period of apparent stability.

statements.text: Maximum drawdown and return standard deviation measure exactly the same feature of a return path.
statements.explanation: Standard deviation measures dispersion, while drawdown measures a path-dependent peak-to-trough loss.

statements.text: Strategy A's frequent ﬂuctuations necessarily make its maximum drawdown larger than Strategy B's.
statements.explanation: The scenario states maximum drawdowns of 6% and 30%, respectively.

statements.text: Drawdown is relevant to the pension because a sufficiently deep loss may trigger governance, liquidity, or behavioral constraints even if the strategy later recovers.
statements.explanation: The path and depth of loss can matter operationally and behaviorally, not only the terminal return.

QF-D2G2Q2.subject: QF

QF-D2G2Q3.scenario: A family office owns two strategies with the same annualized volatility and the same ending wealth. Strategy X suffered a 25% midyear drawdown and then recovered, while Strategy Y remained within 8% of its running peak; the family office may need to withdraw capital during the year.

statements.text: The equal ending wealth proves the investor faced identical path-dependent risk in both strategies.
statements.explanation: Identical endpoints can conceal materially different interim losses and liquidity consequences.

statements.text: Strategy X had the larger maximum drawdown.
statements.explanation: Its 25% maximum drawdown exceeds Strategy Y's stated 8% bound.

statements.text: A reviewer would be wrong to accept the claim that the possibility of an interim withdrawal makes the timing and depth of losses economically relevant.
statements.explanation: The underlying claim is correct and should be accepted. A withdrawal during a deep drawdown may force realization of losses and leave less capital for recovery.

statements.text: After a 25% loss from a peak, a 25% gain from the trough is sufficient to regain that peak.
statements.explanation: A 25% loss requires a gain of 1 / 0.75 - 1, or approximately 33.3%, to recover.

statements.text: Reporting both volatility and drawdown can reveal risk differences hidden by either ending wealth or volatility alone.
statements.explanation: The measures describe different aspects of risk and are complementary here. G3: Sharpe Ratio

QF-D2G2Q3.subject: QF

QF-D2G3Q1.scenario: A client is comparing two funds. Fund A returned 12% with 20% volatility, while Fund B returned 9% with 8% volatility. The risk-free rate was 2%. The client initially prefers Fund A because its raw return was higher.

statements.text: Fund A has the higher excess return.
statements.explanation: Fund A's excess return is 10%, compared with 7% for Fund B.

statements.text: Fund B has the higher Sharpe ratio.
statements.explanation: Fund A's Sharpe ratio is 0.50, while Fund B's is 0.875.

statements.text: Fund A must be the better investment because it earned the higher return.
statements.explanation: Raw return alone does not account for risk.

statements.text: The risk-free rate should not be subtracted from return before computing the Sharpe ratio.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. The Sharpe ratio uses excess return over the risk-free rate.

statements.text: A higher Sharpe ratio indicates more excess return per unit of volatility.
statements.explanation: That is the core interpretation of the Sharpe ratio.

QF-D2G3Q1.subject: QF

QF-D2G3Q2.scenario: A trading desk estimates a strategy's average daily excess return at 0.04% and its daily return standard deviation at 0.80%. The head of trading asks for an annualized Sharpe ratio using 252 trading days and assumes the daily observations are independent and identically distributed for this calculation.

statements.text: The strategy's daily Sharpe ratio is 0.05.
Under the stated assumptions, the annualized Sharpe ratio is not approximately 0.79.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. 0.05 × sqrt(252) is approximately 0.79.

statements.text: Annualizing the Sharpe ratio requires multiplying the daily ratio by 252.
statements.explanation: Under the stated assumptions, the ratio scales by sqrt(252), not 252.

statements.text: The square-root-of-time adjustment relies on assumptions that may fail when returns are autocorrelated or volatility changes over time.
statements.explanation: Dependence and time-varying volatility undermine the simple square-root-of-time rule.

statements.text: If the desk annualizes the mean excess return, it must not also place volatility on a consistent annual scale before forming the ratio.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. The numerator and denominator must use compatible time units.

QF-D2G3Q2.subject: QF

QF-D2G3Q3.scenario: An investment committee compares a liquid equity strategy with a short-volatility strategy. The short-volatility strategy reports a high historical Sharpe ratio because it earned small, steady gains before one rare, severe loss; the chief risk officer warns that the return distribution is highly skewed and fat-tailed.

statements.text: A high historical Sharpe ratio by itself proves that the short-volatility strategy has little tail risk.
statements.explanation: Sharpe summarizes historical excess return relative to volatility and does not prove tail safety.

statements.text: Standard deviation may incompletely describe the risk of a non-normal return distribution.
statements.explanation: Skewness, fat tails, and discontinuous losses are not fully captured by standard deviation.

statements.text: Rare losses can be underrepresented when the estimation window contains few or no tail events.
statements.explanation: A benign sample can make a tail-sensitive strategy appear unusually stable.

statements.text: Two strategies with the same Sharpe ratio must have the same drawdown proﬁle and loss distribution.
statements.explanation: The same ratio can arise from very different return paths and distributions.

statements.text: The committee should supplement Sharpe with measures or scenario analyses that address downside and tail behavior.
statements.explanation: Drawdown, downside metrics, stress tests, and tail analysis can expose risks Sharpe misses. G4: Sortino Ratio and Downside-Focused Metrics

QF-D2G3Q3.subject: QF

QF-D2G4Q1.scenario: A wealth manager compares two funds with the same average return above a 3% minimum acceptable return. Fund A's variability comes mainly from unexpectedly strong gains, while Fund B frequently falls below the 3% target; the client says she is concerned about shortfalls, not positive surprises.

statements.text: The Sortino ratio is not aligned more directly than the Sharpe ratio with the client's stated concern about downside shortfalls.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Sortino relates return above a target to downside deviation below that target.

statements.text: The Sharpe ratio treats upside and downside deviations as contributors to total volatility.
statements.explanation: Total standard deviation does not distinguish favorable from unfavorable deviations.

statements.text: Positive returns far above the target necessarily increase downside deviation.
statements.explanation: Downside deviation focuses on observations below the selected target, not large positive outcomes.

statements.text: Fund A could have a better Sortino ratio than Fund B even if their total standard deviations are similar.
statements.explanation: Similar total volatility can mask materially different downside behavior.

statements.text: A Sortino ratio can be interpreted without specifying or understanding the return threshold used in its calculation.
statements.explanation: The chosen target affects both shortfall identiﬁcation and the resulting ratio.

QF-D2G4Q1.subject: QF

QF-D2G4Q2.scenario: A retirement fund evaluates Strategy X, which has an 8% annual return and 4% downside deviation, and Strategy Y, which has a 10% annual return and 8% downside deviation. Using a 2% annual minimum acceptable return, the investment officer asks which strategy has provided more return above the target per unit of downside risk.

statements.text: Strategy X's Sortino ratio is 1.5.
Strategy Y's Sortino ratio is 1.0.
Strategy Y has the higher Sortino ratio because it has the higher raw return.
statements.explanation: Its greater downside deviation more than offsets its higher raw return in the ratio.

statements.text: On this metric and under the stated inputs, Strategy X has better downside-adjusted performance.
statements.explanation: Strategy X's Sortino ratio of 1.5 exceeds Strategy Y's 1.0.

statements.text: Changing the minimum acceptable return could not change both ratios and potentially affect the comparison.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. The target changes the excess-return numerator and which outcomes count as shortfalls.

QF-D2G4Q2.subject: QF

QF-D2G4Q3.scenario: A hedge fund presents a very high Sortino ratio based on only 18 months of returns, during which no month fell below its chosen 0% target. The due-diligence team knows the strategy sells disaster insurance and can incur rare losses, so it questions whether the ratio is reliable.

statements.text: The absence of observed negative months proves that the strategy has no downside risk.
statements.explanation: An unobserved tail event can still be economically plausible and central to the strategy.

statements.text: With little or no observed downside deviation, the estimated Sortino ratio may be extremely high or not meaningfully deﬁned.
statements.explanation: A near-zero denominator makes the ratio unstable, and a zero denominator prevents an ordinary ﬁnite calculation.

statements.text: A short sample cannot fail to capture the rare events that generate the strategy's principal risk.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Rare-loss strategies may look exceptionally safe during benign windows.

statements.text: Sortino always resolves the non-normal-return limitations associated with the Sharpe ratio.
statements.explanation: Downside focus helps with one limitation but does not eliminate sampling, tail, or estimation problems.

statements.text: Stress testing and a longer, relevant history would help assess the downside exposure not represented in the sample.
statements.explanation: Additional evidence is needed to evaluate losses absent from the observed record. G5: Information Ratio and Active Risk

QF-D2G4Q3.subject: QF

QF-D2G5Q1.scenario: An active equity manager returned 11% while its benchmark returned 8%, and the standard deviation of monthly benchmark-relative returns, annualized, was 6%. The pension board asks whether the manager used active risk efficiently rather than merely beneﬁting from a rising market.

statements.text: The manager's active return was 3%.
statements.explanation: 11% - 8% = 3% active return.

statements.text: The stated tracking error is not 6%.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Tracking error is the volatility of benchmark-relative returns, given here as 6% annualized.

statements.text: The manager's information ratio is 0.50 under the stated annual ﬁgures.
The benchmark's 8% return should be treated as the risk-free rate when computing the manager's Sharpe ratio.
statements.explanation: A benchmark and a risk-free asset serve different roles; benchmark return is used for active-return analysis.

statements.text: A positive information ratio here indicates that realized return exceeded the benchmark per unit of tracking error.
statements.explanation: The numerator is positive active return and the denominator is active risk.

QF-D2G5Q1.subject: QF

QF-D2G5Q2.scenario: A foundation compares Manager A, who beat the benchmark by 2% with 2.5% tracking error, and Manager B, who beat it by 4% with 8% tracking error. The foundation wants consistent benchmark-relative performance and initially favors Manager B because of the larger excess return.

statements.text: Manager A's information ratio is 0.80.
Manager B's information ratio is not 0.50.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. 4% / 8% = 0.50.

statements.text: Manager B used active risk more efficiently because its active return was twice as large.
statements.explanation: Manager B earned more active return but used proportionally much more active risk.

statements.text: Manager A ranks higher by information ratio under the stated ﬁgures.
statements.explanation: 0.80 exceeds 0.50.

statements.text: The information-ratio comparison alone determines which manager is appropriate regardless of the foundation's constraints or conﬁdence in the estimates.
statements.explanation: Mandate constraints, estimation reliability, fees, capacity, and risk tolerance may also affect selection.

QF-D2G5Q2.subject: QF

QF-D2G5Q3.scenario: A global portfolio earned 10% with 12% total volatility, while its policy benchmark earned 9%; the portfolio's tracking error was 2%. The chief investment officer asks analysts to distinguish an information-ratio evaluation from a Sharpe-ratio evaluation and notes that the risk-free rate was 3%.

statements.text: The portfolio's information ratio is 0.50.
statements.explanation: Active return is 1%, and 1% / 2% = 0.50.

statements.text: The portfolio's Sharpe ratio is approximately 0.58.
statements.explanation: (10% - 3%) / 12% is approximately 0.58.

statements.text: Information ratio uses total portfolio volatility as its denominator.
statements.explanation: Information ratio uses tracking error, the volatility of active returns.

statements.text: Sharpe ratio evaluates return above the risk-free rate, whereas information ratio evaluates return above a benchmark.
statements.explanation: The ratios use different reference returns and different risk denominators.

statements.text: A portfolio cannot have a modest Sharpe ratio but a strong information ratio if it tracks a risky benchmark closely and adds consistent value.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Benchmark-relative consistency and total risk-adjusted performance are distinct properties. G6: Risk-Return Tradeoffs

QF-D2G5Q3.subject: QF

QF-D2G6Q1.scenario: A university endowment compares Strategy A, expected to return 9% with 7% volatility, and Strategy B, expected to return 13% with 18% volatility. The endowment needs at least 8% expected return but strongly values spending stability; the investment committee asks whether Strategy B's higher return automatically makes it preferable.

statements.text: Both strategies exceed the stated 8% expected-return requirement.
statements.explanation: Their expected returns are 9% and 13%, both above 8%.

statements.text: Strategy B offers 4 percentage points more expected return and 11 percentage points more estimated volatility.
statements.explanation: The differences are 13% - 9% = 4% in return and 18% - 7% = 11% in volatility.

statements.text: Strategy B is necessarily preferable because rational investors always choose the highest expected return.
statements.explanation: Investors also consider risk, constraints, funding needs, and preferences.

statements.text: A reviewer would be wrong to accept the claim that the endowment's concern about spending stability makes the difference in volatility relevant to its selection.
statements.explanation: The underlying claim is correct and should be accepted. A more volatile asset path may disrupt planned spending or governance tolerance.

statements.text: A risk-adjusted comparison cannot inform the decision but does not eliminate the need to consider the investor's objectives and constraints.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Metrics summarize tradeoffs but do not specify a universal choice for every investor.

QF-D2G6Q1.subject: QF

QF-D2G6Q2.scenario: A leveraged trading strategy earned 18% with 30% volatility, while an unlevered strategy earned 10% with 10% volatility; the risk-free rate was 2%. A portfolio manager argues that the leveraged strategy is superior because it earned nearly twice the raw return.

statements.text: The leveraged strategy's Sharpe ratio is not approximately 0.53.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. (18% - 2%) / 30% is approximately 0.53.

statements.text: The unlevered strategy's Sharpe ratio is 0.80.
The leveraged strategy has both the higher raw return and the higher Sharpe ratio.
statements.explanation: It has the higher return but the lower Sharpe ratio.

statements.text: On a Sharpe-ratio basis, the unlevered strategy used total risk more efficiently over the stated period.
statements.explanation: Its Sharpe ratio of 0.80 exceeds approximately 0.53.

statements.text: The comparison does not by itself address leverage constraints, tail losses, or implementation costs.
statements.explanation: Those considerations are not fully described by the provided return and volatility ﬁgures.

QF-D2G6Q2.subject: QF

QF-D2G6Q3.scenario: A retiree and a well-capitalized proprietary trading ﬁrm are considering the same volatile strategy. The retiree depends on near-term withdrawals and cannot tolerate a 20% drawdown, while the trading ﬁrm has long-dated capital and an explicit 35% drawdown limit; an adviser asks whether one universal ranking should govern both decisions.

statements.text: The same strategy cannot be acceptable to one investor and unsuitable for another because their constraints differ.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Suitability depends on objectives, horizon, liquidity, and loss- bearing capacity.

statements.text: The retiree's withdrawal needs make downside timing and drawdown particularly relevant.
statements.explanation: Losses near withdrawals can impair capital available for both spending and recovery.

statements.text: If the strategy has a positive expected return, the retiree's drawdown limit becomes irrelevant.
statements.explanation: Positive expected return does not prevent an unacceptable interim loss.

statements.text: A single risk-adjusted metric completely captures liquidity needs, horizon, and behavioral tolerance for both investors.
statements.explanation: These constraints require information beyond one summary statistic.

statements.text: Strategy selection should connect measured risk and expected return to the decision maker's capacity and willingness to bear loss.
statements.explanation: Risk-return evaluation is investor-speciﬁc rather than a context-free ranking exercise. G7: Limitations of Risk Metrics

QF-D2G6Q3.subject: QF

QF-D2G7Q1.scenario: A venture fund and a loss-prone trading strategy report the same annual return standard deviation. The venture fund's deviations were mostly unexpectedly large gains, while the trading strategy's deviations were mostly losses; a limited partner asks whether standard deviation alone makes their risk equally attractive.

statements.text: Standard deviation treats equally sized deviations above and below the mean symmetrically.
statements.explanation: Squared deviations enter the calculation regardless of their direction.

statements.text: Equal standard deviations imply that the two return distributions have identical skewness and tail behavior.
statements.explanation: Distributions can share a standard deviation while differing greatly in shape and tails.

statements.text: A downside-focused measure could distinguish features that total standard deviation obscures in this scenario.
statements.explanation: Downside deviation or loss-based analysis can focus on unfavorable outcomes.

statements.text: Large positive surprises can raise measured volatility even though investors may welcome them.
statements.explanation: Upside observations far above the mean increase total measured dispersion.

statements.text: Because standard deviation is imperfect, it contains no useful information about return dispersion.
statements.explanation: It remains informative about dispersion even though it does not capture every dimension of risk.

QF-D2G7Q1.subject: QF

QF-D2G7Q2.scenario: A manager markets a strategy using a Sharpe ratio calculated only over the most recent three calm years, although the strategy performed poorly during an earlier crisis. A due-diligence analyst worries that the chosen window and the manager's presentation choices make the comparison unreliable.

statements.text: A risk-adjusted metric can change materially when the sample period changes.
statements.explanation: Estimated means, volatility, and ratios depend on the observations included.

statements.text: Excluding a relevant stress period cannot make historical risk appear lower and performance appear more favorable.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Removing adverse but relevant outcomes can understate the strategy's historical vulnerability.

statements.text: The most recent three-year window is necessarily the only valid sample because newer data always dominate older evidence.
statements.explanation: Relevance depends on the strategy and regime; recency alone does not make one window uniquely valid.

statements.text: Applying the same disclosed methodology and economically comparable period across strategies improves comparability.
statements.explanation: Consistent methods reduce one important source of presentation bias.

statements.text: A precisely calculated ratio cannot be misleading if the underlying inputs were selectively chosen.
statements.explanation: Arithmetic precision does not cure biased sample selection or inappropriate assumptions.

QF-D2G7Q2.subject: QF

QF-D2G7Q3.scenario: A machine-learning strategy has an excellent backtested Sharpe ratio and low maximum drawdown after extensive hyperparameter tuning. Before allocating capital, the risk committee notes that the estimates are based on one historical sample, returns are fat-tailed, and many model variants were tried.

statements.text: Extensive selection among model variants can inﬂate the reported performance of the chosen backtest.
statements.explanation: Choosing the best result from many trials can capitalize on noise and create selection bias.

statements.text: Historical estimates are guaranteed to remain stable when the strategy begins live trading.
statements.explanation: Market regimes, implementation, estimation error, and overﬁtting can alter live results.

statements.text: Fat-tailed returns make extreme outcomes more plausible than a normal-distribution interpretation may suggest.
statements.explanation: Fat tails assign more probability to extreme outcomes than a comparable normal distribution.

statements.text: Low backtested maximum drawdown establishes a hard upper bound on future drawdown.
statements.explanation: Historical maximum drawdown is an observed sample statistic, not a guaranteed future limit.

statements.text: Out-of-sample testing, sensitivity analysis, and stress testing can provide evidence beyond the headline historical metrics.
statements.explanation: These checks probe robustness and risks that a single optimized backtest can conceal.

QF-D2G7Q3.subject: QF

QF-D3G1Q1.scenario: A family office holds two strategies with similar expected returns and volatilities. Their historical return correlation is - 0.60, and the investment committee asks whether this means one strategy reliably gains whenever the other loses.

statements.text: The negative correlation indicates that the strategies have tended to move in opposite directions, but not in every period.
statements.explanation: Correlation summarizes a tendency toward opposite co-movement, not an exceptionless period-by-period rule.

statements.text: A correlation of -0.60 implies that 60% of one strategy's losses were exactly offset by gains in the other.
statements.explanation: Correlation is a standardized measure of linear co-movement, not an offset percentage.

statements.text: If the correlation moved from -0.60 to +0.60 while other inputs stayed ﬁxed, the volatility of a long-only combination would generally increase.
statements.explanation: A more positive covariance term increases portfolio variance when weights and volatilities are positive.

statements.text: Correlation alone establishes that movements in one strategy cause movements in the other.
statements.explanation: A statistical association does not by itself establish causation.

statements.text: Correlation is not bounded between -1 and +1.
statements.explanation: The statement reverses the correct conclusion. Standardized correlation cannot fall below -1 or exceed +1.

QF-D3G1Q1.subject: QF

QF-D3G1Q2.scenario: A pension fund compares Asset A with two possible diversiﬁers. Asset B has a 0.05 historical correlation with A, while Asset C has a 0.70 correlation with A; the chief investment officer proposes calling B “independent” and C “the same trade.”

statements.text: Asset B's correlation near zero indicates little historical linear co-movement with Asset A.
statements.explanation: A value near zero indicates little linear association in the observed sample.

statements.text: A 0.05 correlation proves that A and B are statistically and economically independent.
statements.explanation: Zero or near-zero linear correlation does not rule out nonlinear dependence or other relationships.

statements.text: All else equal, B would ordinarily offer more diversiﬁcation relative to A than C would.
statements.explanation: Lower correlation generally reduces the covariance contribution to the combined portfolio's variance.

statements.text: A 0.70 correlation means A and C always have returns with the same sign.
statements.explanation: A strong positive correlation allows periods in which returns have different signs.
